Text: Cell membrane The cell membrane, or plasma membrane, is a selectively permeable membrane as an outer boundary of the cell that encloses the cytoplasm.

Text: The membrane serves to separate and protect a cell from its surrounding environment and is made mostly from a lipid bilayer of phospholipids, which are amphiphilic (partly hydrophobic and partly hydrophilic).

Text: Signaling Cell signaling is the process by which a cell interacts with itself, other cells, and the environment.
Label: Human

Text: Typically, the signaling process involves three components: the first messenger (the ligand), the receptor, and the signal itself.
Label: Human

Text: Most cell signaling is chemical in nature, and can occur with neighboring cells or more distant targets.
Label: Human

Text: Signal receptors are complex proteins or tightly bound multimer of proteins, located in the plasma membrane or within the interior.
Label: Human

Text: Each cell is programmed to respond to specific extracellular signal molecules, and this process is the basis of development, tissue repair, immunity, and homeostasis.
Label: Human

Text: Individual cells are able to manage receptor sensitivity including turning them off, and receptors can become less sensitive when they are occupied for long durations.
Label: Human

Text: Errors in signaling interactions may cause diseases such as cancer, autoimmunity, and diabetes.
Label: Human

Text: Protein targeting Protein targeting or protein sorting is the biological mechanism by which proteins are transported to their appropriate destinations within or outside the cell.
Label: Human

Text: Proteins can be targeted to the inner space of an organelle, different intracellular membranes, the plasma membrane, or to the exterior of the cell via secretion.
Label: Human

Text: Correct sorting is crucial for the cell; errors or dysfunction in sorting have been linked to multiple diseases.
Label: Human

Text: DNA repair All cells contain enzyme systems that scan for DNA damage and carry out repair.
Label: Human

Text: Repair is vital to maintain DNA integrity, avoid cell death and errors of replication that could lead to mutation.
Label: Human

Text: Repair processes include nucleotide excision repair, DNA mismatch repair, non-homologous end joining of double-strand breaks, recombinational repair and light-dependent repair (photoreactivation).
Label: Human

Text: Growth and metabolism Between successive cell divisions, cells grow through the functioning of cellular metabolism.
Label: Human

Text: Cell metabolism is the process by which individual cells process nutrient molecules.
Label: Human

Text: Metabolism has two distinct divisions: catabolism, in which the cell breaks down complex molecules to produce energy and reducing power, and anabolism, in which the cell uses energy and reducing power to construct complex molecules and perform other biological functions.
Label: Human

Text: Complex sugars can be broken down into simpler sugar molecules called monosaccharides such as glucose.
Label: Human

Text: Once inside the cell, glucose is broken down to make adenosine triphosphate (ATP), a molecule that possesses readily available energy, through two different pathways.
Label: Human

Text: In plant cells, chloroplasts create sugars by photosynthesis, using the energy of light to join molecules of water and carbon dioxide.
Label: Human

Text: Protein synthesis Cells are capable of synthesizing new proteins, which are essential for the modulation and maintenance of cellular activities.
Label: Human

Text: This process involves the formation of new protein molecules from amino acid building blocks based on information encoded in DNA/RNA.
Label: Human

Text: Protein synthesis generally consists of two major steps: transcription and translation.
Label: Human

Text: Transcription is the process where genetic information in DNA is used to produce a complementary RNA strand.
Label: Human

Text: This RNA strand is then processed to give messenger RNA (mRNA), which is free to migrate into the cytoplasm. mRNA molecules bind to protein-RNA complexes called ribosomes located in the cytosol, where they are translated into polypeptide sequences.
Label: Human

Text: The ribosome mediates the formation of a polypeptide sequence based on the mRNA sequence.
Label: Human

Text: The mRNA sequence directly relates to the polypeptide sequence by binding to transfer RNA (tRNA) adapter molecules in binding pockets within the ribosome.
Label: Human

Text: The new polypeptide chain then folds into a functional three-dimensional protein molecule.
Label: Human

Text: Motility Unicellular organisms can move in order to find food or escape predators.
Label: Human

Text: Common mechanisms of motion include flagella and cilia, and the projection of pseudopodia in amoeboid movement.
Label: Human

Text: Cells in multicellular organisms can move during processes such as wound healing, the immune response, and cancer metastasis.
Label: Human

Text: In wound healing in animals, white blood cells move to the wound site to kill the pathogens causing infection.
Label: Human

Text: Cell motility involves many receptors, crosslinking, bundling, binding, adhesion, motor and other proteins.
Label: Human

Text: The process is divided into three steps: protrusion of the leading edge of the cell, adhesion of the leading edge and de-adhesion at the cell body and rear, and cytoskeletal contraction to pull the cell forward.
Label: Human

Text: Each step is driven by physical forces generated by unique segments of the cytoskeleton.
Label: Human

Text: Cell death Cell death occurs when a cell ceases to carry out its functions, as a result of ageing, or types of cell injury (necrosis).
Label: Human

Text: Programmed cell death, including apoptosis, and autophagy is a natural process of replacing dead cells with new ones.
Label: Human

Text: A separate mode of cellular death is known as a mitotic catastrophe, which occurs during mitosis, following the improper progression of, or entrance to the cell cycle.
Label: Human

Text: Other cell death pathways are described, and include anoikis, pyroptosis, mitoptosis, parthanatos, and necroptosis.
Label: Human

Text: Origins The origin of cells has to do with the origin of life, which began the history of life on Earth.
Label: Human

Text: Small molecules needed for life may have been carried to Earth on meteorites, created at deep-sea vents, or synthesized by lightning in a reducing atmosphere.
Label: Human

Text: There is little experimental data defining what the first self-replicating forms were.
Label: Human

Text: RNA may have been the earliest self-replicating molecule, as it can both store genetic information and catalyze chemical reactions.
Label: Human

Text: This process required an enzyme to catalyze the RNA reactions, which may have been the early peptides that formed in hydrothermal vents.
Label: Human

Text: The early cell membranes were probably simpler and more permeable than later ones, with only a single fatty acid chain per lipid.
Label: Human

Text: Lipids spontaneously form bilayered vesicles in water, and could have preceded RNA.
Label: Human

Text: Eukaryotic cells were created some 2.2 billion years ago in a process called eukaryogenesis.
Label: Human

Text: This is widely agreed to have involved symbiogenesis, in which an archaean and a bacterium came together to create the first eukaryotic common ancestor.
Label: Human

Text: It evolved into a population of single-celled organisms that included the last eukaryotic common ancestor, gaining capabilities along the way.
Label: Human

Text: This cell had a new level of complexity, with a nucleus and facultatively aerobic mitochondria.
Label: Human

Text: It featured at least one centriole and cilium, sex (meiosis and syngamy), peroxisomes, and a dormant cyst with a cell wall of chitin and/or cellulose.
Label: Human

Text: The last eukaryotic common ancestor gave rise to the eukaryotes' crown group, containing the ancestors of animals, fungi, plants, and a diverse range of single-celled organisms.
Label: Human

Text: The green plants were created around 1.6 billion years ago with a second episode of symbiogenesis that added chloroplasts, derived from cyanobacteria.
Label: Human

Text: Multicellularity Multicellular behavior is demonstrated by microorganisms that are cloned from a single cell and form visible microbial colonies.
Label: Human

Text: A microbial consortium of two or more species can form a biofilm by the secretion of extracellular polymeric substances (EPSs).
Label: Human

Text: Slime molds consist of different groups of microorganisms grouped together in a multicellular-like fashion.
Label: Human

Text: The first evidence of multicellularity in an organism comes from cyanobacteria-like organisms that lived between 3 and 3.5 billion years ago.
Label: Human

Text: Cyanobacteria are variable in morphology, filamentous forms exhibit functional cell differentiation such as heterocysts (for nitrogen fixation), akinetes (resting stage cells), and hormogonia (reproductive, motile filaments).
Label: Human

Text: These, together with the intercellular connections they possess, are considered the first signs of multicellularity.
Label: Human

Text: Multicellularity was made possible by the development of the extracellular matrix (ECM) similar in function to the bacterial EPS that consists of extracellular polymeric substances.
Label: Human

Text: EPS enables microbial cell adhesion, and is believed to be the first evolutionary step toward multicellular organisms.
Label: Human

Text: Basement membranes are a type of specialized extracellular matrix that surrounds most animal tissues, and are essential in their formation.
Label: Human

Text: Extracellular matrix components of laminin domains, integrated with other proteins such as cadherins have been described in single-celled motile choanoflagellates that pre-dates the evolutionary emergence of basement membranes, one of the two types of ECM.
Label: Human

Text: The emergence of the basement membrane coincided with the origin of multicellularity.
Label: Human

Text: The evolution of multicellularity from unicellular ancestors has been replicated in the laboratory, in evolution experiments using predation as the selective pressure.
Label: Human

Text: History of research In 1665, Robert Hooke examined a thin slice of cork under his microscope, and saw a structure of small enclosures.
Label: Human

Text: He wrote "I could exceeding plainly perceive it to be all perforated and porous, much like a honeycomb, but that the pores of it were not regular".
Label: Human

Text: To further support his theory, Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann studied cells of both animal and plants.
Label: Human

Text: What they discovered were significant differences between the two types of cells.
Label: Human

Text: This put forth the idea that cells were fundamental to both plants and animals. 1632–1723: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek taught himself to make lenses, constructed basic optical microscopes and drew protozoa, such as Vorticella from rain water, and bacteria from his own mouth. 1665: Robert Hooke discovered cells in cork, then in living plant tissue using an early microscope.
Label: Human

Text: By 1935, he had built an electron microscope with twice the resolution of a light microscope, revealing previously unresolvable organelles. 1981: Lynn Margulis published Symbiosis in Cell Evolution detailing how eukaryotic cells were created by symbiogenesis.
Label: Human

Text: Deoxyribonucleic acid (; DNA) is a polymer composed of two polynucleotide chains that coil around each other to form a double helix.
Label: Human

Text: The polymer carries genetic instructions for the development, functioning, growth and reproduction of all known organisms and many viruses.
Label: Human

Text: Alongside proteins, lipids and complex carbohydrates (polysaccharides), nucleic acids are one of the four major types of macromolecules that are essential for all known forms of life.
Label: Human

Text: The two DNA strands are known as polynucleotides as they are composed of simpler monomeric units called nucleotides.
Label: Human

Text: Each nucleotide is composed of one of four nitrogen-containing nucleobases (cytosine [C], guanine [G], adenine [A] or thymine [T]), a sugar called deoxyribose, and a phosphate group.
Label: Human

Text: The nucleotides are joined to one another in a chain by covalent bonds (known as the phosphodiester linkage) between the sugar of one nucleotide and the phosphate of the next, resulting in an alternating sugar-phosphate backbone.
Label: Human

Text: The nitrogenous bases of the two separate polynucleotide strands are bound together, according to base pairing rules (A with T and C with G), with hydrogen bonds to make double-stranded DNA.
Label: Human

Text: The complementary nitrogenous bases are divided into two groups, the single-ringed pyrimidines and the double-ringed purines.
Label: Human

Text: In DNA, the pyrimidines are thymine and cytosine; the purines are adenine and guanine.
Label: Human

Text: The two strands of DNA run in opposite directions to each other and are thus antiparallel.
Label: Human

Text: It is the sequence of these four nucleobases along the backbone that encodes genetic information.
Label: Human

Text: RNA strands are created using DNA strands as a template in a process called transcription, where DNA bases are exchanged for their corresponding bases except in the case of thymine (T), for which RNA substitutes uracil (U).
Label: Human

Text: Under the genetic code, these RNA strands specify the sequence of amino acids within proteins in a process called translation.
Label: Human

Text: Within eukaryotic cells, DNA is organized into long structures called chromosomes.
Label: Human

Text: Before typical cell division, these chromosomes are duplicated in the process of DNA replication, providing a complete set of chromosomes for each daughter cell.
Label: Human

Text: Eukaryotic organisms (animals, plants, fungi and protists) store most of their DNA inside the cell nucleus as nuclear DNA, and some in the mitochondria as mitochondrial DNA or in chloroplasts as chloroplast DNA.
Label: Human

Text: In contrast, prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) store their DNA only in the cytoplasm, in circular chromosomes.
Label: Human

Text: Within eukaryotic chromosomes, chromatin proteins, such as histones, compact and organize DNA.
Label: Human

Text: These compacting structures guide the interactions between DNA and other proteins, helping control which parts of the DNA are transcribed.
Label: Human

Text: The structure of DNA is dynamic along its length, being capable of coiling into tight loops and other shapes.
Label: Human

Text: In all species it is composed of two helical chains, bound to each other by hydrogen bonds.
Label: Human

Text: Both chains are coiled around the same axis, and have the same pitch of 34 ångströms (3.4 nm).
Label: Human

Text: According to another study, when measured in a different solution, the DNA chain measured 22–26 Å (2.2–2.6 nm) wide, and one nucleotide unit measured 3.3 Å (0.33 nm) long.
Label: Human

Text: DNA does not usually exist as a single strand, but instead as a pair of strands that are held tightly together.
Label: Human

Text: The nucleotide contains both a segment of the backbone of the molecule (which holds the chain together) and a nucleobase (which interacts with the other DNA strand in the helix).
Label: Human

Text: A nucleobase linked to a sugar is called a nucleoside, and a base linked to a sugar and to one or more phosphate groups is called a nucleotide.
Label: Human

Text: A biopolymer comprising multiple linked nucleotides (as in DNA) is called a polynucleotide.
Label: Human

Text: The backbone of the DNA strand is made from alternating phosphate and sugar groups.
Label: Human

Text: The sugars are joined by phosphate groups that form phosphodiester bonds between the third and fifth carbon atoms of adjacent sugar rings.
Label: Human

Text: These are known as the 3′-end (three prime end), and 5′-end (five prime end) carbons, the prime symbol being used to distinguish these carbon atoms from those of the base to which the deoxyribose forms a glycosidic bond.
Label: Human

Text: Therefore, any DNA strand normally has one end at which there is a phosphate group attached to the 5′ carbon of a ribose (the 5′ phosphoryl) and another end at which there is a free hydroxyl group attached to the 3′ carbon of a ribose (the 3′ hydroxyl).
Label: Human

Text: The orientation of the 3′ and 5′ carbons along the sugar-phosphate backbone confers directionality (sometimes called polarity) to each DNA strand.
Label: Human

Text: In a nucleic acid double helix, the direction of the nucleotides in one strand is opposite to their direction in the other strand: the strands are antiparallel.
Label: Human

Text: The asymmetric ends of DNA strands are said to have a directionality of five prime end (5′ ), and three prime end (3′), with the 5′ end having a terminal phosphate group and the 3′ end a terminal hydroxyl group.
Label: Human

Text: One major difference between DNA and RNA is the sugar, with the 2-deoxyribose in DNA being replaced by the related pentose sugar ribose in RNA.
Label: Human

Text: The DNA double helix is stabilized primarily by two forces: hydrogen bonds between nucleotides and base-stacking interactions among aromatic nucleobases.
Label: Human

Text: The four bases found in DNA are adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) and thymine (T).
Label: Human

Text: These four bases are attached to the sugar-phosphate to form the complete nucleotide, as shown for adenosine monophosphate.
Label: Human

Text: Adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine, forming A-T and G-C base pairs.
Label: Human

Text: Nucleobase classification The nucleobases are classified into two types: the purines, A and G, which are fused five- and six-membered heterocyclic compounds, and the pyrimidines, the six-membered rings C and T.
Label: Human

Text: A fifth pyrimidine nucleobase, uracil (U), usually takes the place of thymine in RNA and differs from thymine by lacking a methyl group on its ring.
Label: Human

Text: In addition to RNA and DNA, many artificial nucleic acid analogues have been created to study the properties of nucleic acids, or for use in biotechnology.
Label: Human

Text: The first of these recognized was 5-methylcytosine, which was found in the genome of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in 1925.
Label: Human

Text: The reason for the presence of these noncanonical bases in bacterial viruses (bacteriophages) is to avoid the restriction enzymes present in bacteria.
Label: Human

Text: This enzyme system acts at least in part as a molecular immune system protecting bacteria from infection by viruses.
Label: Human

Text: Modifications of the bases cytosine and adenine, the more common and modified DNA bases, play vital roles in the epigenetic control of gene expression in plants and animals.
Label: Human

Text: Another double helix may be found tracing the spaces, or grooves, between the strands.
Label: Human

Text: As the strands are not symmetrically located with respect to each other, the grooves are unequally sized.
Label: Human

Text: The major groove is 22 ångströms (2.2 nm) wide, while the minor groove is 12 Å (1.2 nm) in width.
Label: Human

Text: Due to the larger width of the major groove, the edges of the bases are more accessible in the major groove than in the minor groove.
Label: Human

Text: As a result, proteins such as transcription factors that can bind to specific sequences in double-stranded DNA usually make contact with the sides of the bases exposed in the major groove.
Label: Human

Text: This situation varies in unusual conformations of DNA within the cell (see below), but the major and minor grooves are always named to reflect the differences in width that would be seen if the DNA was twisted back into the ordinary B form.
Label: Human

Text: Base pairing In a DNA double helix, each type of nucleobase on one strand bonds with just one type of nucleobase on the other strand.
Label: Human

Text: Purines form hydrogen bonds to pyrimidines, with adenine bonding only to thymine in two hydrogen bonds, and cytosine bonding only to guanine in three hydrogen bonds.
Label: Human

Text: This arrangement of two nucleotides binding together across the double helix (from six-carbon ring to six-carbon ring) is called a Watson-Crick base pair.
Label: Human

Text: A Hoogsteen base pair (hydrogen bonding the 6-carbon ring to the 5-carbon ring) is a rare variation of base-pairing.
Label: Human

Text: As hydrogen bonds are not covalent, they can be broken and rejoined relatively easily.
Label: Human

Text: The two strands of DNA in a double helix can thus be pulled apart like a zipper, either by a mechanical force or high temperature.
Label: Human

Text: As a result of this base pair complementarity, all the information in the double-stranded sequence of a DNA helix is duplicated on each strand, which is vital in DNA replication.
Label: Human

Text: This reversible and specific interaction between complementary base pairs is critical for all the functions of DNA in organisms. ssDNA vs. dsDNA Most DNA molecules are actually two polymer strands, bound together in a helical fashion by noncovalent bonds; this double-stranded (dsDNA) structure is maintained largely by the intrastrand base stacking interactions, which are strongest for G,C stacks.
Label: Human

Text: The two strands can come apart—a process known as melting—to form two single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) molecules.
Label: Human

Text: Melting occurs at high temperatures, low salt and high pH (low pH also melts DNA, but since DNA is unstable due to acid depurination, low pH is rarely used).
Label: Human

Text: The stability of the dsDNA form depends not only on the GC-content (% G,C basepairs) but also on sequence (since stacking is sequence specific) and also length (longer molecules are more stable).
Label: Human

Text: The stability can be measured in various ways; a common way is the melting temperature (also called Tm value), which is the temperature at which 50% of the double-strand molecules are converted to single-strand molecules; melting temperature is dependent on ionic strength and the concentration of DNA.
Label: Human

Text: As a result, it is both the percentage of GC base pairs and the overall length of a DNA double helix that determines the strength of the association between the two strands of DNA.
Label: Human

Text: Long DNA helices with a high GC-content have more strongly interacting strands, while short helices with high AT content have more weakly interacting strands.
Label: Human

Text: In biology, parts of the DNA double helix that need to separate easily, such as the TATAAT Pribnow box in some promoters, tend to have a high AT content, making the strands easier to pull apart.
Label: Human

Text: In the laboratory, the strength of this interaction can be measured by finding the melting temperature Tm necessary to break half of the hydrogen bonds.
Label: Human

Text: When all the base pairs in a DNA double helix melt, the strands separate and exist in solution as two entirely independent molecules.
Label: Human

Text: These single-stranded DNA molecules have no single common shape, but some conformations are more stable than others.
Label: Human

Text: Amount In humans, the total female diploid nuclear genome per cell extends for 6.37 Gigabase pairs (Gbp), is 208.23 cm long and weighs 6.51 picograms (pg).
Label: Human

Text: Each DNA polymer can contain hundreds of millions of nucleotides, such as in chromosome 1.
Label: Human

Text: Chromosome 1 is the largest human chromosome with approximately 220 million base pairs, and would be 85 mm long if straightened.
Label: Human

Text: In eukaryotes, in addition to nuclear DNA, there is also mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) which encodes certain proteins used by the mitochondria.
Label: Human

Text: For example, the human mitochondrial DNA forms closed circular molecules, each of which contains 16,569 DNA base pairs, with each such molecule normally containing a full set of the mitochondrial genes.
Label: Human

Text: Each human mitochondrion contains, on average, approximately 5 such mtDNA molecules.
Label: Human

Text: Each human cell contains approximately 100 mitochondria, giving a total number of mtDNA molecules per human cell of approximately 500.
Label: Human

Text: However, the amount of mitochondria per cell also varies by cell type, and an egg cell can contain 100,000 mitochondria, corresponding to up to 1,500,000 copies of the mitochondrial genome (constituting up to 90% of the DNA of the cell).
Label: Human

Text: Sense and antisense A DNA sequence is called a "sense" sequence if it is the same as that of a messenger RNA copy that is translated into protein.
Label: Human

Text: Both sense and antisense sequences can exist on different parts of the same strand of DNA (i.e. both strands can contain both sense and antisense sequences).
Label: Human

Text: In both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, antisense RNA sequences are produced, but the functions of these RNAs are not entirely clear.
Label: Human

Text: One proposal is that antisense RNAs are involved in regulating gene expression through RNA-RNA base pairing.
Label: Human

Text: A few DNA sequences in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and more in plasmids and viruses, blur the distinction between sense and antisense strands by having overlapping genes.
Label: Human

Text: In these cases, some DNA sequences do double duty, encoding one protein when read along one strand, and a second protein when read in the opposite direction along the other strand.
Label: Human

Text: In bacteria, this overlap may be involved in the regulation of gene transcription, while in viruses, overlapping genes increase the amount of information that can be encoded within the small viral genome.
Label: Human

Text: Supercoiling DNA can be twisted like a rope in a process called DNA supercoiling.
Label: Human

Text: With DNA in its "relaxed" state, a strand usually circles the axis of the double helix once every 10.4 base pairs, but if the DNA is twisted the strands become more tightly or more loosely wound.
Label: Human

Text: If the DNA is twisted in the direction of the helix, this is positive supercoiling, and the bases are held more tightly together.
Label: Human

Text: If they are twisted in the opposite direction, this is negative supercoiling, and the bases come apart more easily.
Label: Human

Text: In nature, most DNA has slight negative supercoiling that is introduced by enzymes called topoisomerases.
Label: Human

Text: These enzymes are also needed to relieve the twisting stresses introduced into DNA strands during processes such as transcription and DNA replication.
Label: Human

Text: Alternative DNA structures DNA exists in many possible conformations that include A-DNA, B-DNA, and Z-DNA forms, although only B-DNA and Z-DNA have been directly observed in functional organisms.
Label: Human

Text: The conformation that DNA adopts depends on the hydration level, DNA sequence, the amount and direction of supercoiling, chemical modifications of the bases, the type and concentration of metal ions, and the presence of polyamines in solution.
Label: Human

Text: The first published reports of A-DNA X-ray diffraction patterns—and also B-DNA—used analyses based on Patterson functions that provided only a limited amount of structural information for oriented fibers of DNA.
Label: Human

Text: An alternative analysis was proposed by Wilkins et al. in 1953 for the in vivo B-DNA X-ray diffraction-scattering patterns of highly hydrated DNA fibers in terms of squares of Bessel functions.
Label: Human

Text: In the same journal, James Watson and Francis Crick presented their molecular modeling analysis of the DNA X-ray diffraction patterns to suggest that the structure was a double helix.
Label: Human

Text: Although the B-DNA form is most common under the conditions found in cells, it is not a well-defined conformation but a family of related DNA conformations that occur at the high hydration levels present in cells.
Label: Human

Text: Their corresponding X-ray diffraction and scattering patterns are characteristic of molecular paracrystals with a significant degree of disorder.
Label: Human

Text: Compared to B-DNA, the A-DNA form is a wider right-handed spiral, with a shallow, wide minor groove and a narrower, deeper major groove.
Label: Human

Text: The A form occurs under non-physiological conditions in partly dehydrated samples of DNA, while in the cell it may be produced in hybrid pairings of DNA and RNA strands, and in enzyme-DNA complexes.
Label: Human

Text: Segments of DNA where the bases have been chemically modified by methylation may undergo a larger change in conformation and adopt the Z form.
Label: Human

Text: Here, the strands turn about the helical axis in a left-handed spiral, the opposite of the more common B form.
Label: Human

Text: These unusual structures can be recognized by specific Z-DNA binding proteins and may be involved in the regulation of transcription.
Label: Human

Text: Alternative DNA chemistry For many years, exobiologists have proposed the existence of a shadow biosphere, a postulated microbial biosphere of Earth that uses radically different biochemical and molecular processes than currently known life.
Label: Human

Text: One of the proposals was the existence of lifeforms that use arsenic instead of phosphorus in DNA.
Label: Human

Text: A report in 2010 of the possibility in the bacterium GFAJ-1 was announced, though the research was disputed, and evidence suggests the bacterium actively prevents the incorporation of arsenic into the DNA backbone and other biomolecules.
Label: Human

Text: Quadruplex structures At the ends of the linear chromosomes are specialized regions of DNA called telomeres.
Label: Human

Text: The main function of these regions is to allow the cell to replicate chromosome ends using the enzyme telomerase, as the enzymes that normally replicate DNA cannot copy the extreme 3′ ends of chromosomes.
Label: Human

Text: These specialized chromosome caps also help protect the DNA ends, and stop the DNA repair systems in the cell from treating them as damage to be corrected.
Label: Human

Text: In human cells, telomeres are usually lengths of single-stranded DNA containing several thousand repeats of a simple TTAGGG sequence.
Label: Human

Text: These guanine-rich sequences may stabilize chromosome ends by forming structures of stacked sets of four-base units, rather than the usual base pairs found in other DNA molecules.
Label: Human

Text: These flat four-base units then stack on top of each other to form a stable G-quadruplex structure.
Label: Human

Text: These structures are stabilized by hydrogen bonding between the edges of the bases and chelation of a metal ion in the centre of each four-base unit.
Label: Human

Text: Other structures can also be formed, with the central set of four bases coming from either a single strand folded around the bases, or several different parallel strands, each contributing one base to the central structure.
Label: Human

Text: In addition to these stacked structures, telomeres also form large loop structures called telomere loops, or T-loops.
Label: Human

Text: Here, the single-stranded DNA curls around in a long circle stabilized by telomere-binding proteins.
Label: Human

Text: At the very end of the T-loop, the single-stranded telomere DNA is held onto a region of double-stranded DNA by the telomere strand disrupting the double-helical DNA and base pairing to one of the two strands.
Label: Human

Text: Branched DNA In DNA, fraying occurs when non-complementary regions exist at the end of an otherwise complementary double-strand of DNA.
Label: Human

Text: However, branched DNA can occur if a third strand of DNA is introduced and contains adjoining regions able to hybridize with the frayed regions of the pre-existing double-strand.
Label: Human

Text: Although the simplest example of branched DNA involves only three strands of DNA, complexes involving additional strands and multiple branches are also possible.
Label: Human

Text: Branched DNA can be used in nanotechnology to construct geometric shapes, see the section on uses in technology below.
Label: Human

Text: Artificial bases Several artificial nucleobases have been synthesized, and successfully incorporated in the eight-base DNA analogue named Hachimoji DNA.
Label: Human

Text: Dubbed S, B, P, and Z, these artificial bases are capable of bonding with each other in a predictable way (S–B and P–Z), maintain the double helix structure of DNA, and be transcribed to RNA.
Label: Human

Text: Their existence could be seen as an indication that there is nothing special about the four natural nucleobases that evolved on Earth.
Label: Human

Text: On the other hand, DNA is tightly related to RNA which does not only act as a transcript of DNA but also performs as molecular machines many tasks in cells.
Label: Human

Text: It has been shown that to allow to create all possible structures at least four bases are required for the corresponding RNA, while a higher number is also possible but this would be against the natural principle of least effort.
Label: Human

Text: Acidity The phosphate groups of DNA give it similar acidic properties to phosphoric acid and it can be considered as a strong acid.
Label: Human

Text: It will be fully ionized at a normal cellular pH, releasing protons which leave behind negative charges on the phosphate groups.
Label: Human

Text: These negative charges protect DNA from breakdown by hydrolysis by repelling nucleophiles which could hydrolyze it.
Label: Human

Text: Macroscopic appearance Pure DNA extracted from cells forms white, stringy clumps.
Label: Human

Text: Chemical modifications and altered DNA packaging Base modifications and DNA packaging The expression of genes is influenced by how the DNA is packaged in chromosomes, in a structure called chromatin.
Label: Human

Text: Base modifications can be involved in packaging, with regions that have low or no gene expression usually containing high levels of methylation of cytosine bases.
Label: Human

Text: DNA packaging and its influence on gene expression can also occur by covalent modifications of the histone protein core around which DNA is wrapped in the chromatin structure or else by remodeling carried out by chromatin remodeling complexes (see Chromatin remodeling).
Label: Human

Text: There is, further, crosstalk between DNA methylation and histone modification, so they can coordinately affect chromatin and gene expression.
Label: Human

Text: For one example, cytosine methylation produces 5-methylcytosine, which is important for X-inactivation of chromosomes.
Label: Human

Text: The average level of methylation varies between organisms—the worm Caenorhabditis elegans lacks cytosine methylation, while vertebrates have higher levels, with up to 1% of their DNA containing 5-methylcytosine.
Label: Human

Text: Despite the importance of 5-methylcytosine, it can deaminate to leave a thymine base, so methylated cytosines are particularly prone to mutations.
Label: Human

Text: Other base modifications include adenine methylation in bacteria, the presence of 5-hydroxymethylcytosine in the brain, and the glycosylation of uracil to produce the "J-base" in kinetoplastids.
Label: Human

Text: Damage DNA can be damaged by many sorts of mutagens, which change the DNA sequence.
Label: Human

Text: Mutagens include oxidizing agents, alkylating agents and also high-energy electromagnetic radiation such as ultraviolet light and X-rays.
Label: Human

Text: For example, UV light can damage DNA by producing thymine dimers, which are cross-links between pyrimidine bases.
Label: Human

Text: On the other hand, oxidants such as free radicals or hydrogen peroxide produce multiple forms of damage, including base modifications, particularly of guanosine, and double-strand breaks.
Label: Human

Text: A typical human cell contains about 150,000 bases that have suffered oxidative damage.
Label: Human

Text: Of these oxidative lesions, the most dangerous are double-strand breaks, as these are difficult to repair and can produce point mutations, insertions, deletions from the DNA sequence, and chromosomal translocations.
Label: Human

Text: Because of inherent limits in the DNA repair mechanisms, if humans lived long enough, they would all eventually develop cancer.
Label: Human

Text: DNA damages that are naturally occurring, due to normal cellular processes that produce reactive oxygen species, the hydrolytic activities of cellular water, etc., also occur frequently.
Label: Human

Text: Although most of these damages are repaired, in any cell some DNA damage may remain despite the action of repair processes.
Label: Human

Text: These remaining DNA damages accumulate with age in mammalian postmitotic tissues.
Label: Human

Text: Many mutagens fit into the space between two adjacent base pairs, this is called intercalation.
Label: Human

Text: Most intercalators are aromatic and planar molecules; examples include ethidium bromide, acridines, daunomycin, and doxorubicin.
Label: Human

Text: For an intercalator to fit between base pairs, the bases must separate, distorting the DNA strands by unwinding of the double helix.
Label: Human

Text: This inhibits both transcription and DNA replication, causing toxicity and mutations.
Label: Human

Text: As a result, DNA intercalators may be carcinogens, and in the case of thalidomide, a teratogen.
Label: Human

Text: Others such as benzo[a]pyrene diol epoxide and aflatoxin form DNA adducts that induce errors in replication.
Label: Human

Text: Nevertheless, due to their ability to inhibit DNA transcription and replication, other similar toxins are also used in chemotherapy to inhibit rapidly growing cancer cells.
Label: Human

Text: Biological functions DNA usually occurs as linear chromosomes in eukaryotes, and circular chromosomes in prokaryotes.
Label: Human

Text: The set of chromosomes in a cell makes up its genome; the human genome has approximately 3 billion base pairs of DNA arranged into 46 chromosomes.
Label: Human

Text: The information carried by DNA is held in the sequence of pieces of DNA called genes.
Label: Human

Text: Transmission of genetic information in genes is achieved via complementary base pairing.
Label: Human

Text: For example, in transcription, when a cell uses the information in a gene, the DNA sequence is copied into a complementary RNA sequence through the attraction between the DNA and the correct RNA nucleotides.
Label: Human

Text: Usually, this RNA copy is then used to make a matching protein sequence in a process called translation, which depends on the same interaction between RNA nucleotides.
Label: Human

Text: In an alternative fashion, a cell may copy its genetic information in a process called DNA replication.
Label: Human

Text: The details of these functions are covered in other articles; here the focus is on the interactions between DNA and other molecules that mediate the function of the genome.
Label: Human

Text: Genomes Genomic DNA is tightly and orderly packed in the process called DNA condensation, to fit the small available volumes of the cell.
Label: Human

Text: In eukaryotes, DNA is located in the cell nucleus, with small amounts in mitochondria and chloroplasts.
Label: Human

Text: In prokaryotes, the DNA is held within an irregularly shaped body in the cytoplasm called the nucleoid.
Label: Human

Text: The functional genetic information in a genome is located in genes, regulatory sequences, origins of replication, centromeres, telomeres, and segments required for the three-dimensional structure of chromatin.
Label: Human

Text: In many complex eukaryotes, only a small fraction of the total sequence is devoted to the various functional elements.
Label: Human

Text: For example, in humans less than 10% of the genome has a defined functional role and the rest (90%) is probably junk DNA. (See also [Non-coding DNA].) Transcription and translation A gene is a sequence of DNA that contains genetic information and can influence the phenotype of an organism.
Label: Human

Text: Within a gene, the sequence of bases along a DNA strand defines a messenger RNA sequence, which then defines one or more protein sequences.
Label: Human

Text: The relationship between the nucleotide sequences of genes and the amino-acid sequences of proteins is determined by the rules of translation, known collectively as the genetic code.
Label: Human

Text: The genetic code consists of three-letter 'words' called codons formed from a sequence of three nucleotides (e.g., ACT, CAG, TTT).
Label: Human

Text: In transcription, the codons of a gene are copied into messenger RNA by RNA polymerase.
Label: Human

Text: This RNA copy is then decoded by a ribosome that reads the RNA sequence by base-pairing the messenger RNA to transfer RNA, which carries amino acids.
Label: Human

Text: Since there are 4 bases in 3-letter combinations, there are 64 possible codons (43 combinations).
Label: Human

Text: These encode the twenty standard amino acids, giving most amino acids more than one possible codon.
Label: Human

Text: There are also three 'stop' or 'nonsense' codons signifying the end of the coding region; these are the TAG, TAA, and TGA codons, (UAG, UAA, and UGA on the mRNA).
Label: Human

Text: Replication Cell division is essential for an organism to grow, but, when a cell divides, it must replicate the DNA in its genome so that the two daughter cells have the same genetic information as their parent.
Label: Human

Text: The double-stranded structure of DNA provides a simple mechanism for DNA replication.
Label: Human

Text: Here, the two strands are separated and then each strand's complementary DNA sequence is recreated by an enzyme called DNA polymerase.
Label: Human

Text: This enzyme makes the complementary strand by finding the correct base through complementary base pairing and bonding it onto the original strand.
Label: Human

Text: As DNA polymerases can only extend a DNA strand in a 5′ to 3′ direction, different mechanisms are used to copy the antiparallel strands of the double helix.
Label: Human

Text: In this way, the base on the old strand dictates which base appears on the new strand, and the cell ends up with a perfect copy of its DNA.
Label: Human

Text: Extracellular nucleic acids Naked extracellular DNA (eDNA), most of it released by cell death, is nearly ubiquitous in the environment.
Label: Human

Text: Its concentration in soil may be as high as 2 μg/L, and its concentration in natural aquatic environments may be as high at 88 μg/L.
Label: Human

Text: Various possible functions have been proposed for eDNA: it may be involved in horizontal gene transfer; it may provide nutrients; and it may act as a buffer to recruit or titrate ions or antibiotics.
Label: Human

Text: Extracellular DNA acts as a functional extracellular matrix component in the biofilms of several bacterial species.
Label: Human

Text: It may act as a recognition factor to regulate the attachment and dispersal of specific cell types in the biofilm; it may contribute to biofilm formation; and it may contribute to the biofilm's physical strength and resistance to biological stress.
Label: Human

Text: Cell-free fetal DNA is found in the blood of the mother, and can be sequenced to determine a great deal of information about the developing fetus.
Label: Human

Text: Under the name of environmental DNA eDNA has seen increased use in the natural sciences as a survey tool for ecology, monitoring the movements and presence of species in water, air, or on land, and assessing an area's biodiversity.
Label: Human

Text: Interactions with proteins All the functions of DNA depend on interactions with proteins.
Label: Human

Text: These protein interactions can be non-specific, or the protein can bind specifically to a single DNA sequence.
Label: Human

Text: Enzymes can also bind to DNA and of these, the polymerases that copy the DNA base sequence in transcription and DNA replication are particularly important.
Label: Human

Text: DNA-binding proteins Structural proteins that bind DNA are well-understood examples of non-specific DNA-protein interactions.
Label: Human

Text: In eukaryotes, this structure involves DNA binding to a complex of small basic proteins called histones, while in prokaryotes multiple types of proteins are involved.
Label: Human

Text: The histones form a disk-shaped complex called a nucleosome, which contains two complete turns of double-stranded DNA wrapped around its surface.
Label: Human

Text: These non-specific interactions are formed through basic residues in the histones, making ionic bonds to the acidic sugar-phosphate backbone of the DNA, and are thus largely independent of the base sequence.
Label: Human

Text: Chemical modifications of these basic amino acid residues include methylation, phosphorylation, and acetylation.
Label: Human

Text: These chemical changes alter the strength of the interaction between the DNA and the histones, making the DNA more or less accessible to transcription factors and changing the rate of transcription.
Label: Human

Text: Other non-specific DNA-binding proteins in chromatin include the high-mobility group proteins, which bind to bent or distorted DNA.
Label: Human

Text: These proteins are important in bending arrays of nucleosomes and arranging them into the larger structures that make up chromosomes.
Label: Human

Text: A distinct group of DNA-binding proteins is the DNA-binding proteins that specifically bind single-stranded DNA.
Label: Human

Text: In humans, replication protein A is the best-understood member of this family and is used in processes where the double helix is separated, including DNA replication, recombination, and DNA repair.
Label: Human

Text: These binding proteins seem to stabilize single-stranded DNA and protect it from forming stem-loops or being degraded by nucleases.
Label: Human

Text: The most intensively studied of these are the various transcription factors, which are proteins that regulate transcription.
Label: Human

Text: Each transcription factor binds to one particular set of DNA sequences and activates or inhibits the transcription of genes that have these sequences close to their promoters.
Label: Human

Text: Firstly, they can bind the RNA polymerase responsible for transcription, either directly or through other mediator proteins; this locates the polymerase at the promoter and allows it to begin transcription.
Label: Human

Text: Alternatively, transcription factors can bind enzymes that modify the histones at the promoter.
Label: Human

Text: As these DNA targets can occur throughout an organism's genome, changes in the activity of one type of transcription factor can affect thousands of genes.
Label: Human

Text: Consequently, these proteins are often the targets of the signal transduction processes that control responses to environmental changes or cellular differentiation and development.
Label: Human

Text: The specificity of these transcription factors' interactions with DNA come from the proteins making multiple contacts to the edges of the DNA bases, allowing them to "read" the DNA sequence.
Label: Human

Text: Most of these base-interactions are made in the major groove, where the bases are most accessible.
Label: Human

Text: DNA-modifying enzymes Nucleases and ligases Nucleases are enzymes that cut DNA strands by catalyzing the hydrolysis of the phosphodiester bonds.
Label: Human

Text: Nucleases that hydrolyse nucleotides from the ends of DNA strands are called exonucleases, while endonucleases cut within strands.
Label: Human

Text: The most frequently used nucleases in molecular biology are the restriction endonucleases, which cut DNA at specific sequences.
Label: Human

Text: For instance, the EcoRV enzyme shown to the left recognizes the 6-base sequence 5′-GATATC-3′ and makes a cut at the horizontal line.
Label: Human

Text: In nature, these enzymes protect bacteria against phage infection by digesting the phage DNA when it enters the bacterial cell, acting as part of the restriction modification system.
Label: Human

Text: In technology, these sequence-specific nucleases are used in molecular cloning and DNA fingerprinting.
Label: Human

Text: Ligases are particularly important in lagging strand DNA replication, as they join the short segments of DNA produced at the replication fork into a complete copy of the DNA template.
Label: Human

Text: Topoisomerases and helicases Topoisomerases are enzymes with both nuclease and ligase activity.
Label: Human

Text: Some of these enzymes work by cutting the DNA helix and allowing one section to rotate, thereby reducing its level of supercoiling; the enzyme then seals the DNA break.
Label: Human

Text: Other types of these enzymes are capable of cutting one DNA helix and then passing a second strand of DNA through this break, before rejoining the helix.
Label: Human

Text: Topoisomerases are required for many processes involving DNA, such as DNA replication and transcription.
Label: Human

Text: They use the chemical energy in nucleoside triphosphates, predominantly adenosine triphosphate (ATP), to break hydrogen bonds between bases and unwind the DNA double helix into single strands.
Label: Human

Text: These enzymes are essential for most processes where enzymes need to access the DNA bases.
Label: Human

Text: Polymerases Polymerases are enzymes that synthesize polynucleotide chains from nucleoside triphosphates.
Label: Human

Text: The sequence of their products is created based on existing polynucleotide chains—which are called templates.
Label: Human

Text: These enzymes function by repeatedly adding a nucleotide to the 3′ hydroxyl group at the end of the growing polynucleotide chain.
Label: Human

Text: In the active site of these enzymes, the incoming nucleoside triphosphate base-pairs to the template: this allows polymerases to accurately synthesize the complementary strand of their template.
Label: Human

Text: In DNA replication, DNA-dependent DNA polymerases make copies of DNA polynucleotide chains.
Label: Human

Text: To preserve biological information, it is essential that the sequence of bases in each copy are precisely complementary to the sequence of bases in the template strand.
Label: Human

Text: Here, the polymerase recognizes the occasional mistakes in the synthesis reaction by the lack of base pairing between the mismatched nucleotides.
Label: Human

Text: If a mismatch is detected, a 3′ to 5′ exonuclease activity is activated and the incorrect base removed.
Label: Human

Text: In most organisms, DNA polymerases function in a large complex called the replisome that contains multiple accessory subunits, such as the DNA clamp or helicases.
Label: Human

Text: RNA-dependent DNA polymerases are a specialized class of polymerases that copy the sequence of an RNA strand into DNA.
Label: Human

Text: They include reverse transcriptase, which is a viral enzyme involved in the infection of cells by retroviruses, and telomerase, which is required for the replication of telomeres.
Label: Human

Text: Telomerase is an unusual polymerase because it contains its own RNA template as part of its structure.
Label: Human

Text: Telomeres prevent fusion of the ends of neighboring chromosomes and protect chromosome ends from damage.
Label: Human

Text: Transcription is carried out by a DNA-dependent RNA polymerase that copies the sequence of a DNA strand into RNA.
Label: Human

Text: To begin transcribing a gene, the RNA polymerase binds to a sequence of DNA called a promoter and separates the DNA strands.
Label: Human

Text: It then copies the gene sequence into a messenger RNA transcript until it reaches a region of DNA called the terminator, where it halts and detaches from the DNA.
Label: Human

Text: As with human DNA-dependent DNA polymerases, RNA polymerase II, the enzyme that transcribes most of the genes in the human genome, operates as part of a large protein complex with multiple regulatory and accessory subunits.
Label: Human

Text: Genetic recombination A DNA helix usually does not interact with other segments of DNA, and in human cells, the different chromosomes even occupy separate areas in the nucleus called "chromosome territories".
Label: Human

Text: This physical separation of different chromosomes is important for the ability of DNA to function as a stable repository for information, as one of the few times chromosomes interact is in chromosomal crossover which occurs during sexual reproduction, when genetic recombination occurs.
Label: Human

Text: Chromosomal crossover is when two DNA helices break, swap a section and then rejoin.
Label: Human

Text: Recombination allows chromosomes to exchange genetic information and produces new combinations of genes, which increases the efficiency of natural selection and can be important in the rapid evolution of new proteins.
Label: Human

Text: Genetic recombination can also be involved in DNA repair, particularly in the cell's response to double-strand breaks.
Label: Human

Text: The most common form of chromosomal crossover is homologous recombination, where the two chromosomes involved share very similar sequences.
Label: Human

Text: Non-homologous recombination can be damaging to cells, as it can produce chromosomal translocations and genetic abnormalities.
Label: Human

Text: The recombination reaction is catalyzed by enzymes known as recombinases, such as RAD51.
Label: Human

Text: The first step in recombination is a double-stranded break caused by either an endonuclease or damage to the DNA.
Label: Human

Text: A series of steps catalyzed in part by the recombinase then leads to joining of the two helices by at least one Holliday junction, in which a segment of a single strand in each helix is annealed to the complementary strand in the other helix.
Label: Human

Text: The Holliday junction is a tetrahedral junction structure that can be moved along the pair of chromosomes, swapping one strand for another.
Label: Human

Text: The recombination reaction is then halted by cleavage of the junction and re-ligation of the released DNA.
Label: Human

Text: The north–south cleavage nicks both strands of DNA, while the east–west cleavage has one strand of DNA intact.
Label: Human

Text: The formation of a Holliday junction during recombination makes it possible for genetic diversity, genes to exchange on chromosomes, and expression of wild-type viral genomes.
Label: Human

Text: Evolution DNA contains the genetic information that allows all forms of life to function, grow and reproduce.
Label: Human

Text: However, it is unclear how long in the 4-billion-year history of life DNA has performed this function, as it has been proposed that the earliest forms of life may have used RNA as their genetic material.
Label: Human

Text: RNA may have acted as the central part of early cell metabolism as it can both transmit genetic information and carry out catalysis as part of ribozymes.
Label: Human

Text: This ancient RNA world where nucleic acid would have been used for both catalysis and genetics may have influenced the evolution of the current genetic code based on four nucleotide bases.
Label: Human

Text: This would occur, since the number of different bases in such an organism is a trade-off between a small number of bases increasing replication accuracy and a large number of bases increasing the catalytic efficiency of ribozymes.
Label: Human

Text: However, there is no direct evidence of ancient genetic systems, as recovery of DNA from most fossils is impossible because DNA survives in the environment for less than one million years, and slowly degrades into short fragments in solution.
Label: Human

Text: Claims for older DNA have been made, most notably a report of the isolation of a viable bacterium from a salt crystal 250 million years old, but these claims are controversial.
Label: Human

Text: Building blocks of DNA (adenine, guanine, and related organic molecules) may have been formed extraterrestrially in outer space.
Label: Human

Text: Complex DNA and RNA organic compounds of life, including uracil, cytosine, and thymine, have also been formed in the laboratory under conditions mimicking those found in outer space, using starting chemicals, such as pyrimidine, found in meteorites.
Label: Human

Text: Pyrimidine, like polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), the most carbon-rich chemical found in the universe, may have been formed in red giants or in interstellar cosmic dust and gas clouds.
Label: Human

Text: Ancient DNA has been recovered from ancient organisms at a timescale where genome evolution can be directly observed, including from extinct organisms up to millions of years old, such as the woolly mammoth.
Label: Human

Text: Uses in technology Genetic engineering Methods have been developed to purify DNA from organisms, such as phenol-chloroform extraction, and to manipulate it in the laboratory, such as restriction digests and the polymerase chain reaction.
Label: Human

Text: Modern biology and biochemistry make intensive use of these techniques in recombinant DNA technology.
Label: Human

Text: Recombinant DNA is a man-made DNA sequence that has been assembled from other DNA sequences.
Label: Human

Text: They can be transformed into organisms in the form of plasmids or in the appropriate format, by using a viral vector.
Label: Human

Text: The genetically modified organisms produced can be used to produce products such as recombinant proteins, used in medical research, or be grown in agriculture.
Label: Human

Text: DNA profiling Forensic scientists can use DNA in blood, semen, skin, saliva or hair found at a crime scene to identify a matching DNA of an individual, such as a perpetrator.
Label: Human

Text: In DNA profiling, the lengths of variable sections of repetitive DNA, such as short tandem repeats and minisatellites, are compared between people.
Label: Human

Text: This method is usually an extremely reliable technique for identifying a matching DNA.
Label: Human

Text: However, identification can be complicated if the scene is contaminated with DNA from several people.
Label: Human

Text: DNA profiling was developed in 1984 by British geneticist Sir Alec Jeffreys, and first used in forensic science to convict Colin Pitchfork in the 1988 Enderby murders case.
Label: Human

Text: The development of forensic science and the ability to now obtain genetic matching on minute samples of blood, skin, saliva, or hair has led to re-examining many cases.
Label: Human

Text: Evidence can now be uncovered that was scientifically impossible at the time of the original examination.
Label: Human

Text: Combined with the removal of the double jeopardy law in some places, this can allow cases to be reopened where prior trials have failed to produce sufficient evidence to convince a jury.
Label: Human

Text: People charged with serious crimes may be required to provide a sample of DNA for matching purposes.
Label: Human

Text: The most obvious defense to DNA matches obtained forensically is to claim that cross-contamination of evidence has occurred.
Label: Human

Text: This has resulted in meticulous strict handling procedures with new cases of serious crime.
Label: Human

Text: DNA profiling is also used successfully to positively identify victims of mass casualty incidents, bodies or body parts in serious accidents, and individual victims in mass war graves, via matching to family members.
Label: Human

Text: DNA profiling is also used in DNA paternity testing to determine if someone is the biological parent or grandparent of a child with the probability of parentage is typically 99.99% when the alleged parent is biologically related to the child.
Label: Human

Text: Usually DNA sequencing are carried out after birth, but there are new methods to test paternity while a mother is still pregnant.
Label: Human

Text: DNA enzymes or catalytic DNA Deoxyribozymes, also called DNAzymes or catalytic DNA, were first discovered in 1994.
Label: Human

Text: They are mostly single stranded DNA sequences isolated from a large pool of random DNA sequences through a combinatorial approach called in vitro selection or systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX).
Label: Human

Text: DNAzymes catalyze variety of chemical reactions including RNA-DNA cleavage, RNA-DNA ligation, amino acids phosphorylation-dephosphorylation, carbon-carbon bond formation, etc.
Label: Human

Text: DNAzymes can enhance catalytic rate of chemical reactions up to 100,000,000,000-fold over the uncatalyzed reaction.
Label: Human

Text: The most extensively studied class of DNAzymes is RNA-cleaving types which have been used to detect different metal ions and designing therapeutic agents.
Label: Human

Text: Several metal-specific DNAzymes have been reported including the GR-5 DNAzyme (lead-specific), the CA1-3 DNAzymes (copper-specific), the 39E DNAzyme (uranyl-specific) and the NaA43 DNAzyme (sodium-specific).
Label: Human

Text: The NaA43 DNAzyme, which is reported to be more than 10,000-fold selective for sodium over other metal ions, was used to make a real-time sodium sensor in cells.
Label: Human

Text: Bioinformatics Bioinformatics involves the development of techniques to store, data mine, search and manipulate biological data, including DNA nucleic acid sequence data.
Label: Human

Text: These have led to widely applied advances in computer science, especially string searching algorithms, machine learning, and database theory.
Label: Human

Text: String searching or matching algorithms, which find an occurrence of a sequence of letters inside a larger sequence of letters, were developed to search for specific sequences of nucleotides.
Label: Human

Text: The DNA sequence may be aligned with other DNA sequences to identify homologous sequences and locate the specific mutations that make them distinct.
Label: Human

Text: These techniques, especially multiple sequence alignment, are used in studying phylogenetic relationships and protein function.
Label: Human

Text: Data sets representing entire genomes' worth of DNA sequences, such as those produced by the Human Genome Project, are difficult to use without the annotations that identify the locations of genes and regulatory elements on each chromosome.
Label: Human

Text: Regions of DNA sequence that have the characteristic patterns associated with protein- or RNA-coding genes can be identified by gene finding algorithms, which allow researchers to predict the presence of particular gene products and their possible functions in an organism even before they have been isolated experimentally.
Label: Human

Text: Entire genomes may also be compared, which can shed light on the evolutionary history of particular organism and permit the examination of complex evolutionary events.
Label: Human

Text: DNA nanotechnology DNA nanotechnology uses the unique molecular recognition properties of DNA and other nucleic acids to create self-assembling branched DNA complexes with useful properties.
Label: Human

Text: DNA is thus used as a structural material rather than as a carrier of biological information.
Label: Human

Text: This has led to the creation of two-dimensional periodic lattices (both tile-based and using the DNA origami method) and three-dimensional structures in the shapes of polyhedra.
Label: Human

Text: Nanomechanical devices and algorithmic self-assembly have also been demonstrated, and these DNA structures have been used to template the arrangement of other molecules such as gold nanoparticles and streptavidin proteins.
Label: Human

Text: DNA and other nucleic acids are the basis of aptamers, synthetic oligonucleotide ligands for specific target molecules used in a range of biotechnology and biomedical applications.
Label: Human

Text: History and anthropology Because DNA collects mutations over time, which are then inherited, it contains historical information, and, by comparing DNA sequences, geneticists can infer the evolutionary history of organisms, their phylogeny.
Label: Human

Text: If DNA sequences within a species are compared, population geneticists can learn the history of particular populations.
Label: Human

Text: Information storage DNA as a storage device for information has enormous potential since it has much higher storage density compared to electronic devices.
Label: Human

Text: However, high costs, slow read and write times (memory latency), and insufficient reliability has prevented its practical use.
Label: Human

Text: History DNA was first isolated by the Swiss physician Friedrich Miescher who, in 1869, discovered a microscopic substance in the pus of discarded surgical bandages.
Label: Human

Text: In 1878, Albrecht Kossel isolated the non-protein component of "nuclein", nucleic acid, and later isolated its five primary nucleobases.
Label: Human

Text: In 1909, Phoebus Levene identified the base, sugar, and phosphate nucleotide unit of RNA (then named "yeast nucleic acid").
Label: Human

Text: Levene suggested that DNA consisted of a string of four nucleotide units linked together through the phosphate groups ("tetranucleotide hypothesis").
Label: Human

Text: In 1927, Nikolai Koltsov proposed that inherited traits would be inherited via a "giant hereditary molecule" made up of "two mirror strands that would replicate in a semi-conservative fashion using each strand as a template".
Label: Human

Text: In 1928, Frederick Griffith in his experiment discovered that traits of the "smooth" form of Pneumococcus could be transferred to the "rough" form of the same bacteria by mixing killed "smooth" bacteria with the live "rough" form.
Label: Human

Text: This system provided the first clear suggestion that DNA carries genetic information.
Label: Human

Text: In 1933, while studying virgin sea urchin eggs, Jean Brachet suggested that DNA is found in the cell nucleus and that RNA is present exclusively in the cytoplasm.
Label: Human

Text: At the time, "yeast nucleic acid" (RNA) was thought to occur only in plants, while "thymus nucleic acid" (DNA) only in animals.
Label: Human

Text: The latter was thought to be a tetramer, with the function of buffering cellular pH.
Label: Human

Text: In 1937, William Astbury produced the first X-ray diffraction patterns that showed that DNA had a regular structure.
Label: Human

Text: In 1943, Oswald Avery, along with co-workers Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty, identified DNA as the transforming principle, supporting Griffith's suggestion (Avery–MacLeod–McCarty experiment).
Label: Human

Text: Erwin Chargaff developed and published observations now known as Chargaff's rules, stating that in DNA from any species of any organism, the amount of guanine should be equal to cytosine and the amount of adenine should be equal to thymine.
Label: Human

Text: By 1951, Alec Todd and collaborators at the University of Cambridge had determined by biochemical methods how the backbone of DNA is structured via the successive linking of carbon atoms 3 and 5 of the sugar to phosphates.
Label: Human

Text: Todd would later be awarded the 1957 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this and other discoveries related to DNA.

Text: Late in 1951, Francis Crick started working with James Watson at the Cavendish Laboratory within the University of Cambridge.

Text: DNA's role in heredity was confirmed in 1952 when Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase in the Hershey–Chase experiment showed that DNA is the genetic material of the enterobacteria phage T2.

Text: On 28 February 1953 Crick interrupted patrons' lunchtime at The Eagle pub in Cambridge, England to announce that he and Watson had "discovered the secret of life".

Text: The 25 April 1953 issue of the journal Nature published a series of five articles giving the Watson and Crick double-helix structure DNA and evidence supporting it.

Label: Human
