Text: Photosynthesis ( FOH-tə-SINTH-ə-sis) is a system of biological processes by which photopigment-bearing autotrophic organisms, such as most plants, algae and cyanobacteria, convert light energy — typically from sunlight — into the chemical energy necessary to fuel their metabolism.
Label: Human

Text: The term photosynthesis usually refers to oxygenic photosynthesis, a process that releases oxygen as a byproduct of water splitting.
Label: Human

Text: Photosynthetic organisms store the converted chemical energy within the bonds of intracellular organic compounds (complex compounds containing carbon), typically carbohydrates like sugars (mainly glucose, fructose and sucrose), starches, phytoglycogen and cellulose.
Label: Human

Text: When needing to use this stored energy, an organism's cells then metabolize the organic compounds through cellular respiration.
Label: Human

Text: Photosynthesis plays a critical role in producing and maintaining the oxygen content of the Earth's atmosphere, and it supplies most of the biological energy necessary for complex life on Earth.
Label: Human

Text: Some organisms also perform anoxygenic photosynthesis, which does not produce oxygen.
Label: Human

Text: Some bacteria (e.g. purple bacteria) use bacteriochlorophyll to split hydrogen sulfide as a reductant instead of water, releasing sulfur instead of oxygen, which was a dominant form of photosynthesis in the euxinic Canfield oceans during the Boring Billion.
Label: Human

Text: Such archaeal photosynthesis might have been the earliest form of photosynthesis that evolved on Earth, as far back as the Paleoarchean, preceding that of cyanobacteria (see Purple Earth hypothesis).
Label: Human

Text: While the details may differ between species, the process always begins when light energy is absorbed by the reaction centers, proteins that contain photosynthetic pigments or chromophores.
Label: Human

Text: In plants, these pigments are chlorophylls (a porphyrin derivative that absorbs the red and blue spectra of light, thus reflecting green) held inside chloroplasts, abundant in leaf cells.
Label: Human

Text: In these light-dependent reactions, some energy is used to strip electrons from suitable substances, such as water, producing oxygen gas.
Label: Human

Text: The hydrogen freed by the splitting of water is used in the creation of two important molecules that participate in energetic processes: reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) and ATP.
Label: Human

Text: In plants, algae, and cyanobacteria, sugars are synthesized by a subsequent sequence of light-independent reactions called the Calvin cycle.
Label: Human

Text: In this process, atmospheric carbon dioxide is incorporated into already existing organic compounds, such as ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP).
Label: Human

Text: Using the ATP and NADPH produced by the light-dependent reactions, the resulting compounds are then reduced and removed to form further carbohydrates, such as glucose.
Label: Human

Text: In other bacteria, different mechanisms like the reverse Krebs cycle are used to achieve the same end.
Label: Human

Text: The first photosynthetic organisms probably evolved early in the evolutionary history of life using reducing agents such as hydrogen or hydrogen sulfide, rather than water, as sources of electrons.
Label: Human

Text: Cyanobacteria appeared later; the excess oxygen they produced contributed directly to the oxygenation of the Earth, which rendered the evolution of complex life possible.
Label: Human

Text: The average rate of energy captured by global photosynthesis is approximately 130 terawatts, which is about eight times the total power consumption of human civilization.
Label: Human

Text: Photosynthetic organisms also convert around 100–115 billion tons (91–104 Pg petagrams, or billions of metric tons), of carbon into biomass per year.
Label: Human

Text: Photosynthesis was discovered in 1779 by Jan Ingenhousz who showed that plants need light, not just soil and water.
Label: Human

Text: Overview Most photosynthetic organisms are photoautotrophs, which means that they are able to synthesize food directly from carbon dioxide and water using energy from light.
Label: Human

Text: However, not all organisms use carbon dioxide as a source of carbon atoms to carry out photosynthesis; photoheterotrophs use organic compounds, rather than carbon dioxide, as a source of carbon.
Label: Human

Text: This oxygenic photosynthesis is by far the most common type of photosynthesis used by living organisms.
Label: Human

Text: Some shade-loving plants (sciophytes) produce such low levels of oxygen during photosynthesis that they use all of it themselves instead of releasing it to the atmosphere.
Label: Human

Text: Although there are some differences between oxygenic photosynthesis in plants, algae, and cyanobacteria, the overall process is quite similar in these organisms.
Label: Human

Text: There are also many varieties of anoxygenic photosynthesis, used mostly by bacteria, which consume carbon dioxide but do not release oxygen or which produce elemental sulfur instead of molecular oxygen.
Label: Human

Text: Carbon dioxide is converted into sugars in a process called carbon fixation; photosynthesis captures energy from sunlight to convert carbon dioxide into carbohydrates.
Label: Human

Text: In general outline, photosynthesis is the opposite of cellular respiration: while photosynthesis is a process of reduction of carbon dioxide to carbohydrates, cellular respiration is the oxidation of carbohydrates or other nutrients to carbon dioxide.
Label: Human

Text: Nutrients used in cellular respiration include carbohydrates, amino acids and fatty acids.
Label: Human

Text: These nutrients are oxidized to produce carbon dioxide and water, and to release chemical energy to drive the organism's metabolism.
Label: Human

Text: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are distinct processes, as they take place through different sequences of chemical reactions and in different cellular compartments (cellular respiration in mitochondria).
Label: Human

Text: In the first stage, light-dependent reactions or light reactions capture the energy of light and use it to make the hydrogen carrier NADPH and the energy-storage molecule ATP.
Label: Human

Text: During the second stage, the light-independent reactions use these products to capture and reduce carbon dioxide.
Label: Human

Text: Most organisms that use oxygenic photosynthesis use visible light for the light-dependent reactions, although at least three use shortwave infrared or, more specifically, far-red radiation.
Label: Human

Text: Some archaea use a simpler method that employs a pigment similar to those used for vision in animals.
Label: Human

Text: The bacteriorhodopsin changes its configuration in response to sunlight, acting as a proton pump.
Label: Human

Text: This produces a proton gradient more directly, which is then converted to chemical energy.
Label: Human

Text: The process does not involve carbon dioxide fixation and does not release oxygen, and seems to have evolved separately from the more common types of photosynthesis.
Label: Human

Text: Photosynthetic membranes and organelles In photosynthetic bacteria, the proteins that gather light for photosynthesis are embedded in cell membranes.
Label: Human

Text: However, the membrane may be tightly folded into cylindrical sheets called thylakoids, or bunched up into round vesicles called intracytoplasmic membranes.
Label: Human

Text: These structures can fill most of the interior of a cell, giving the membrane a very large surface area and therefore increasing the amount of light that the bacteria can absorb.
Label: Human

Text: In plants and algae, photosynthesis takes place in organelles called chloroplasts.
Label: Human

Text: This membrane is composed of a phospholipid inner membrane, a phospholipid outer membrane, and an intermembrane space.
Label: Human

Text: Embedded within the stroma are stacks of thylakoids (grana), which are the site of photosynthesis.
Label: Human

Text: The thylakoid itself is enclosed by the thylakoid membrane, and within the enclosed volume is a lumen or thylakoid space.
Label: Human

Text: Embedded in the thylakoid membrane are integral and peripheral membrane protein complexes of the photosynthetic system.
Label: Human

Text: The green part of the light spectrum is not absorbed but is reflected, which is the reason that most plants have a green color.
Label: Human

Text: Besides chlorophyll, plants also use pigments such as carotenes and xanthophylls.
Label: Human

Text: Algae also use chlorophyll, but various other pigments are present, such as phycocyanin, carotenes, and xanthophylls in green algae, phycoerythrin in red algae (rhodophytes) and fucoxanthin in brown algae and diatoms resulting in a wide variety of colors.
Label: Human

Text: These pigments are embedded in plants and algae in complexes called antenna proteins.
Label: Human

Text: Although all cells in the green parts of a plant have chloroplasts, the majority of those are found in specially adapted structures called leaves.
Label: Human

Text: Certain species adapted to conditions of strong sunlight and aridity, such as many Euphorbia and cactus species, have their main photosynthetic organs in their stems.
Label: Human

Text: The cells in the interior tissues of a leaf, called the mesophyll, can contain between 450,000 and 800,000 chloroplasts for every square millimeter of leaf.
Label: Human

Text: The surface of the leaf is coated with a water-resistant waxy cuticle that protects the leaf from excessive evaporation of water and decreases the absorption of ultraviolet or blue light to minimize heating.
Label: Human

Text: The transparent epidermis layer allows light to pass through to the palisade mesophyll cells where most of the photosynthesis takes place.
Label: Human

Text: Light-dependent reactions In the light-dependent reactions, one molecule of the pigment chlorophyll absorbs one photon and loses one electron.
Label: Human

Text: This electron is taken up by a modified form of chlorophyll called pheophytin, which passes the electron to a quinone molecule, starting the flow of electrons down an electron transport chain that leads to the ultimate reduction of NADP to NADPH.
Label: Human

Text: In addition, this creates a proton gradient (energy gradient) across the chloroplast membrane, which is used by ATP synthase in the synthesis of ATP.
Label: Human

Text: The chlorophyll molecule ultimately regains the electron it lost when a water molecule is split in a process called photolysis, which releases oxygen.
Label: Human

Text: The overall equation for the light-dependent reactions under the conditions of non-cyclic electron flow in green plants is: Not all wavelengths of light can support photosynthesis.
Label: Human

Text: The photosynthetic action spectrum depends on the type of accessory pigments present.
Label: Human

Text: For example, in green plants, the action spectrum resembles the absorption spectrum for chlorophylls and carotenoids with absorption peaks in violet-blue and red light.
Label: Human

Text: In red algae, the action spectrum is blue-green light, which allows these algae to use the blue end of the spectrum to grow in the deeper waters that filter out the longer wavelengths (red light) used by above-ground green plants.
Label: Human

Text: The non-absorbed part of the light spectrum is what gives photosynthetic organisms their color (e.g., green plants, red algae, purple bacteria) and is the least effective for photosynthesis in the respective organisms.
Label: Human

Text: Z scheme In plants, light-dependent reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplasts where they drive the synthesis of ATP and NADPH.
Label: Human

Text: In the non-cyclic reaction, the photons are captured in the light-harvesting antenna complexes of photosystem II by chlorophyll and other accessory pigments (see diagram "Z-scheme").
Label: Human

Text: The absorption of a photon by the antenna complex loosens an electron by a process called photoinduced charge separation.
Label: Human

Text: The antenna system is at the core of the chlorophyll molecule of the photosystem II reaction center.
Label: Human

Text: That loosened electron is taken up by the primary electron-acceptor molecule, pheophytin.
Label: Human

Text: As the electrons are shuttled through an electron transport chain (the so-called Z-scheme shown in the diagram), a chemiosmotic potential is generated by pumping proton cations (H+) across the membrane and into the thylakoid space.
Label: Human

Text: An ATP synthase enzyme uses that chemiosmotic potential to make ATP during photophosphorylation, whereas NADPH is a product of the terminal redox reaction in the Z-scheme.
Label: Human

Text: The electron is then passed along a chain of electron acceptors to which it transfers some of its energy.
Label: Human

Text: The energy delivered to the electron acceptors is used to move hydrogen ions across the thylakoid membrane into the lumen.
Label: Human

Text: The electron is eventually used to reduce the coenzyme NADP with an H+ to NADPH (which has functions in the light-independent reaction); at that point, the path of that electron ends.
Label: Human

Text: The cyclic reaction is similar to that of the non-cyclic but differs in that it generates only ATP, and no reduced NADP (NADPH) is created.
Label: Human

Text: Once the electron is displaced from the photosystem, the electron is passed down the electron acceptor molecules and returns to photosystem I, from where it was emitted, hence the name cyclic reaction.
Label: Human

Text: Water photolysis Linear electron transport through a photosystem will leave the reaction center of that photosystem oxidized.
Label: Human

Text: Elevating another electron will first require re-reduction of the reaction center.
Label: Human

Text: The excited electrons lost from the reaction center (P700) of photosystem I are replaced by transfer from plastocyanin, whose electrons come from electron transport through photosystem II.
Label: Human

Text: Photosystem II, as the first step of the Z-scheme, requires an external source of electrons to reduce its oxidized chlorophyll a reaction center.
Label: Human

Text: The source of electrons for photosynthesis in green plants and cyanobacteria is water.
Label: Human

Text: Two water molecules are oxidized by the energy of four successive charge-separation reactions of photosystem II to yield a molecule of diatomic oxygen and four hydrogen ions.
Label: Human

Text: The electrons yielded are transferred to a redox-active tyrosine residue that is oxidized by the energy of P680+.
Label: Human

Text: This resets the ability of P680 to absorb another photon and release another photo-dissociated electron.
Label: Human

Text: The oxidation of water is catalyzed in photosystem II by a redox-active structure that contains four manganese ions and a calcium ion; this oxygen-evolving complex binds two water molecules and contains the four oxidizing equivalents that are used to drive the water-oxidizing reaction (Kok's S-state diagrams).
Label: Human

Text: The hydrogen ions are released in the thylakoid lumen and therefore contribute to the transmembrane chemiosmotic potential that leads to ATP synthesis.
Label: Human

Text: Oxygen is a waste product of light-dependent reactions, but the majority of organisms on Earth use oxygen and its energy for cellular respiration, including photosynthetic organisms.
Label: Human

Text: Light-independent reactions Calvin cycle In the light-independent (or "dark") reactions, the enzyme RuBisCO captures CO2 from the atmosphere and, in a process called the Calvin cycle, uses the newly formed NADPH and releases three-carbon sugars, which are later combined to form sucrose and starch.
Label: Human

Text: The overall equation for the light-independent reactions in green plants is Carbon fixation produces the three-carbon sugar intermediate, which is then converted into the final carbohydrate products.
Label: Human

Text: The simple carbon sugars photosynthesis produces are then used to form other organic compounds, such as the building material cellulose, the precursors for lipid and amino acid biosynthesis, or as a fuel in cellular respiration.
Label: Human

Text: The latter occurs not only in plants but also in animals when the carbon and energy from plants is passed through a food chain.
Label: Human

Text: The fixation or reduction of carbon dioxide is a process in which carbon dioxide combines with a five-carbon sugar, ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate, to yield two molecules of a three-carbon compound, glycerate 3-phosphate, also known as 3-phosphoglycerate.
Label: Human

Text: Glycerate 3-phosphate, in the presence of ATP and NADPH produced during the light-dependent stages, is reduced to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate.
Label: Human

Text: This product is also referred to as 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (PGAL) or, more generically, as triose phosphate.
Label: Human

Text: Most (five out of six molecules) of the glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate produced are used to regenerate ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate so the process can continue.
Label: Human

Text: The triose phosphates not thus "recycled" often condense to form hexose phosphates, which ultimately yield sucrose, starch, and cellulose, as well as glucose and fructose.
Label: Human

Text: The sugars produced during carbon metabolism yield carbon skeletons that can be used for other metabolic reactions like the production of amino acids and lipids.
Label: Human

Text: Carbon concentrating mechanisms On land In hot and dry conditions, plants close their stomata to prevent water loss.
Label: Human

Text: Under these conditions, CO2 will decrease and oxygen gas, produced by the light reactions of photosynthesis, will increase, causing an increase of photorespiration by the oxygenase activity of ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RuBisCO) and decrease in carbon fixation.
Label: Human

Text: Some plants have evolved mechanisms to increase the CO2 concentration in the leaves under these conditions.
Label: Human

Text: Plants that use the C4 carbon fixation process chemically fix carbon dioxide in the cells of the mesophyll by adding it to the three-carbon molecule phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP), a reaction catalyzed by an enzyme called PEP carboxylase, creating the four-carbon organic acid oxaloacetic acid.
Label: Human

Text: Oxaloacetic acid or malate synthesized by this process is then translocated to specialized bundle sheath cells where the enzyme RuBisCO and other Calvin cycle enzymes are located, and where CO2 released by decarboxylation of the four-carbon acids is then fixed by RuBisCO activity to the three-carbon 3-phosphoglyceric acids.
Label: Human

Text: The physical separation of RuBisCO from the oxygen-generating light reactions reduces photorespiration and increases CO2 fixation and, thus, the photosynthetic capacity of the leaf.
Label: Human

Text: C4 plants can produce more sugar than C3 plants in conditions of high light and temperature.
Label: Human

Text: Many important crop plants are C4 plants, including maize, sorghum, sugarcane, and millet.
Label: Human

Text: Plants that do not use PEP-carboxylase in carbon fixation are called C3 plants because the primary carboxylation reaction, catalyzed by RuBisCO, produces the three-carbon 3-phosphoglyceric acids directly in the Calvin-Benson cycle.
Label: Human

Text: Over 90% of plants use C3 carbon fixation, compared to 3% that use C4 carbon fixation; however, the evolution of C4 in over sixty plant lineages makes it a striking example of convergent evolution.
Label: Human

Text: C2 photosynthesis, which involves carbon-concentration by selective breakdown of photorespiratory glycine, is both an evolutionary precursor to C4 and a useful carbon-concentrating mechanism in its own right.
Label: Human

Text: Xerophytes, such as cacti and most succulents, also use PEP carboxylase to capture carbon dioxide in a process called Crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM).
Label: Human

Text: In contrast to C4 metabolism, which spatially separates the CO2 fixation to PEP from the Calvin cycle, CAM temporally separates these two processes.
Label: Human

Text: CAM plants have a different leaf anatomy from C3 plants, and fix the CO2 at night, when their stomata are open.
Label: Human

Text: CAM plants store the CO2 mostly in the form of malic acid via carboxylation of phosphoenolpyruvate to oxaloacetate, which is then reduced to malate.
Label: Human

Text: Decarboxylation of malate during the day releases CO2 inside the leaves, thus allowing carbon fixation to 3-phosphoglycerate by RuBisCO.
Label: Human

Text: Calcium-oxalate-accumulating plants, such as Amaranthus hybridus and Colobanthus quitensis, show a variation of photosynthesis where calcium oxalate crystals function as dynamic carbon pools, supplying carbon dioxide (CO2) to photosynthetic cells when stomata are partially or totally closed.
Label: Human

Text: Under stress conditions (e.g., water deficit), oxalate released from calcium oxalate crystals is converted to CO2 by an oxalate oxidase enzyme, and the produced CO2 can support the Calvin cycle reactions.
Label: Human

Text: Reactive hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), the byproduct of oxalate oxidase reaction, can be neutralized by catalase.
Label: Human

Text: Alarm photosynthesis represents a photosynthetic variant to be added to the well-known C4 and CAM pathways.
Label: Human

Text: However, alarm photosynthesis, in contrast to these pathways, operates as a biochemical pump that collects carbon from the organ interior (or from the soil) and not from the atmosphere.
Label: Human

Text: In water Cyanobacteria possess carboxysomes, which increase the concentration of CO2 around RuBisCO to increase the rate of photosynthesis.
Label: Human

Text: An enzyme, carbonic anhydrase, located within the carboxysome, releases CO2 from dissolved hydrocarbonate ions (HCO−3).
Label: Human

Text: Before the CO2 can diffuse out, RuBisCO concentrated within the carboxysome quickly sponges it up.
Label: Human

Text: HCO−3 ions are made from CO2 outside the cell by another carbonic anhydrase and are actively pumped into the cell by a membrane protein.
Label: Human

Text: They cannot cross the membrane as they are charged, and within the cytosol they turn back into CO2 very slowly without the help of carbonic anhydrase.
Label: Human

Text: This causes the HCO−3 ions to accumulate within the cell from where they diffuse into the carboxysomes.
Label: Human

Text: Order and kinetics The overall process of photosynthesis takes place in four stages: Efficiency Plants usually convert light into chemical energy with a photosynthetic efficiency of 3–6%.
Label: Human

Text: Absorbed light that is unconverted is dissipated primarily as heat, with a small fraction (1–2%) reemitted as chlorophyll fluorescence at longer (redder) wavelengths.
Label: Human

Text: This fact allows measurement of the light reaction of photosynthesis by using chlorophyll fluorometers.
Label: Human

Text: Actual plants' photosynthetic efficiency varies with the frequency of the light being converted, light intensity, temperature, and proportion of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, and can vary from 0.1% to 8%.
Label: Human

Text: By comparison, solar panels convert light into electric energy at an efficiency of approximately 6–20% for mass-produced panels, and above 40% in laboratory devices.
Label: Human

Text: Scientists are studying photosynthesis in hopes of developing plants with increased yield.
Label: Human

Text: The efficiency of both light and dark reactions can be measured, but the relationship between the two can be complex.
Label: Human

Text: For example, the light reaction creates ATP and NADPH energy molecules, which C3 plants can use for carbon fixation or photorespiration.
Label: Human

Text: For this reason, it is not uncommon for authors to differentiate between work done under non-photorespiratory conditions and under photorespiratory conditions.
Label: Human

Text: Chlorophyll fluorescence of photosystem II can measure the light reaction, and infrared gas analyzers can measure the dark reaction.
Label: Human

Text: An integrated chlorophyll fluorometer and gas exchange system can investigate both light and dark reactions when researchers use the two separate systems together.
Label: Human

Text: Infrared gas analyzers and some moisture sensors are sensitive enough to measure the photosynthetic assimilation of CO2 and of ΔH2O using reliable methods.
Label: Human

Text: CO2 is commonly measured in μmols/(m2/s), parts per million, or volume per million; and H2O is commonly measured in mmols/(m2/s) or in mbars.
Label: Human

Text: By measuring CO2 assimilation, ΔH2O, leaf temperature, barometric pressure, leaf area, and photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), it becomes possible to estimate, "A" or carbon assimilation, "E" or transpiration, "gs" or stomatal conductance, and "Ci" or intracellular CO2.
Label: Human

Text: However, it is more common to use chlorophyll fluorescence for plant stress measurement, where appropriate, because the most commonly used parameters FV/FM and Y(II) or F/FM' can be measured in a few seconds, allowing the investigation of larger plant populations.
Label: Human

Text: Gas exchange systems that offer control of CO2 levels, above and below ambient, allow the common practice of measurement of A/Ci curves, at different CO2 levels, to characterize a plant's photosynthetic response.
Label: Human

Text: Integrated chlorophyll fluorometer – gas exchange systems allow a more precise measure of photosynthetic response and mechanisms.
Label: Human

Text: While standard gas exchange photosynthesis systems can measure Ci, or substomatal CO2 levels, the addition of integrated chlorophyll fluorescence measurements allows a more precise measurement of CC, the estimation of CO2 concentration at the site of carboxylation in the chloroplast, to replace Ci.
Label: Human

Text: CO2 concentration in the chloroplast becomes possible to estimate with the measurement of mesophyll conductance or gm using an integrated system.
Label: Human

Text: Photosynthesis measurement systems are not designed to directly measure the amount of light the leaf absorbs, but analysis of chlorophyll fluorescence, P700- and P515-absorbance, and gas exchange measurements reveal detailed information about, e.g., the photosystems, quantum efficiency and the CO2 assimilation rates.
Label: Human

Text: With some instruments, even wavelength dependency of the photosynthetic efficiency can be analyzed.
Label: Human

Text: A phenomenon known as quantum walk increases the efficiency of the energy transport of light significantly.
Label: Human

Text: In the photosynthetic cell of an alga, bacterium, or plant, there are light-sensitive molecules called chromophores arranged in an antenna-shaped structure called a photocomplex.
Label: Human

Text: When a photon is absorbed by a chromophore, it is converted into a quasiparticle referred to as an exciton, which jumps from chromophore to chromophore towards the reaction center of the photocomplex, a collection of molecules that traps its energy in a chemical form accessible to the cell's metabolism.
Label: Human

Text: The exciton's wave properties enable it to cover a wider area and try out several possible paths simultaneously, allowing it to instantaneously "choose" the most efficient route, where it will have the highest probability of arriving at its destination in the minimum possible time.
Label: Human

Text: Because that quantum walking takes place at temperatures far higher than quantum phenomena usually occur, it is only possible over very short distances.
Label: Human

Text: Obstacles in the form of destructive interference cause the particle to lose its wave properties for an instant before it regains them once again after it is freed from its locked position through a classic "hop".
Label: Human

Text: The movement of the electron towards the photo center is therefore covered in a series of conventional hops and quantum walks.
Label: Human

Text: Evolution Fossils of what are thought to be filamentous photosynthetic organisms have been dated at 3.4 billion years old.
Label: Human

Text: More recent studies also suggest that photosynthesis may have begun about 3.4 billion years ago, though the first direct evidence of photosynthesis comes from thylakoid membranes preserved in 1.75-billion-year-old cherts.
Label: Human

Text: Oxygenic photosynthesis is the main source of oxygen in the Earth's atmosphere, and its earliest appearance is sometimes referred to as the oxygen catastrophe.
Label: Human

Text: Geological evidence suggests that oxygenic photosynthesis, such as that in cyanobacteria, became important during the Paleoproterozoic era around two billion years ago.
Label: Human

Text: Modern photosynthesis in plants and most photosynthetic prokaryotes is oxygenic, using water as an electron donor, which is oxidized to molecular oxygen in the photosynthetic reaction center.
Label: Human

Text: Symbiosis and the origin of chloroplasts Several groups of animals have formed symbiotic relationships with photosynthetic algae.
Label: Human

Text: Scientists presume that this is due to the particularly simple body plans and large surface areas of these animals compared to their volumes.
Label: Human

Text: In addition, a few marine mollusks, such as Elysia viridis and Elysia chlorotica, also maintain a symbiotic relationship with chloroplasts they capture from the algae in their diet and then store in their bodies (see Kleptoplasty).
Label: Human

Text: This allows the mollusks to survive solely by photosynthesis for several months at a time.
Label: Human

Text: Some of the genes from the plant cell nucleus have even been transferred to the slugs, so that the chloroplasts can be supplied with proteins they need to survive.
Label: Human

Text: Chloroplasts have many similarities with photosynthetic bacteria, including a circular chromosome, prokaryotic-type ribosome, and similar proteins in the photosynthetic reaction center.
Label: Human

Text: The endosymbiotic theory suggests that photosynthetic bacteria were acquired (by endocytosis) by early eukaryotic cells to form the first plant cells.
Label: Human

Text: Therefore, chloroplasts may be photosynthetic bacteria that adapted to life inside plant cells.
Label: Human

Text: Like mitochondria, chloroplasts possess their own DNA, separate from the nuclear DNA of their plant host cells and the genes in this chloroplast DNA resemble those found in cyanobacteria.
Label: Human

Text: DNA in chloroplasts codes for redox proteins such as those found in the photosynthetic reaction centers.
Label: Human

Text: The CoRR Hypothesis proposes that this co-location of genes with their gene products is required for redox regulation of gene expression, and accounts for the persistence of DNA in bioenergetic organelles.
Label: Human

Text: Archaeplastida and the photosynthetic Paulinella got their plastids, which are surrounded by two membranes, through primary endosymbiosis in two separate events, by engulfing a cyanobacterium.
Label: Human

Text: The plastids in all the other groups have either a red or green algal origin, and are referred to as the "red lineages" and the "green lineages".
Label: Human

Text: The only known exception is the ciliate Pseudoblepharisma tenue, which in addition to its plastids that originated from green algae also has a purple sulfur bacterium as symbiont.
Label: Human

Text: In dinoflagellates and euglenids the plastids are surrounded by three membranes, and in the remaining lines by four.
Label: Human

Text: A nucleomorph, remnants of the original algal nucleus located between the inner and outer membranes of the plastid, is present in the cryptophytes (from a red alga) and chlorarachniophytes (from a green alga).
Label: Human

Text: Some dinoflagellates that lost their photosynthetic ability later regained it again through new endosymbiotic events with different algae.
Label: Human

Text: While able to perform photosynthesis, many of these eukaryotic groups are mixotrophs and practice heterotrophy to various degrees.
Label: Human

Text: Photosynthetic prokaryotic lineages Early photosynthetic systems, such as those in green and purple sulfur and green and purple nonsulfur bacteria, are thought to have been anoxygenic, and used various other molecules than water as electron donors.
Label: Human

Text: Green and purple sulfur bacteria are thought to have used hydrogen and sulfur as electron donors.
Label: Human

Text: Green nonsulfur bacteria used various amino and other organic acids as electron donors.
Label: Human

Text: The use of these molecules is consistent with the geological evidence that Earth's early atmosphere was highly reducing at that time.
Label: Human

Text: With a possible exception of Heimdallarchaeota, photosynthesis is not found in archaea.
Label: Human

Text: Haloarchaea are photoheterotrophic; they can absorb energy from the sun, but do not harvest carbon from the atmosphere and are therefore not photosynthetic.
Label: Human

Text: Instead of chlorophyll they use rhodopsins, which convert light-energy to ion gradients but cannot mediate electron transfer reactions.
Label: Human

Text: In bacteria eight photosynthetic lineages are currently known: Cyanobacteria, the only prokaryotes performing oxygenic photosynthesis and the only prokaryotes that contain two types of photosystems (type I (RCI), also known as Fe-S type, and type II (RCII), also known as quinone type).
Label: Human

Text: The seven remaining prokaryotes have anoxygenic photosynthesis and use versions of either type I or type II.
Label: Human

Text: The geological record indicates that this transforming event took place early in Earth's history, at least 2450–2320 million years ago (Ma), and, it is speculated, much earlier.
Label: Human

Text: Because the Earth's atmosphere contained almost no oxygen during the estimated development of photosynthesis, it is believed that the first photosynthetic cyanobacteria did not generate oxygen.
Label: Human

Text: Available evidence from geobiological studies of Archean (>2500 Ma) sedimentary rocks indicates that life existed 3500 Ma, but the question of when oxygenic photosynthesis evolved is still unanswered.
Label: Human

Text: A clear paleontological window on cyanobacterial evolution opened about 2000 Ma, revealing an already-diverse biota of cyanobacteria.
Label: Human

Text: Cyanobacteria remained the principal primary producers of oxygen throughout the Proterozoic Eon (2500–543 Ma), in part because the redox structure of the oceans favored photoautotrophs capable of nitrogen fixation.
Label: Human

Text: Green algae joined cyanobacteria as the major primary producers of oxygen on continental shelves near the end of the Proterozoic, but only with the Mesozoic (251–66 Ma) radiations of dinoflagellates, coccolithophorids, and diatoms did the primary production of oxygen in marine shelf waters take modern form.
Label: Human

Text: Cyanobacteria remain critical to marine ecosystems as primary producers of oxygen in oceanic gyres, as agents of biological nitrogen fixation, and, in modified form, as the plastids of marine algae.
Label: Human

Text: Experimental history Discovery Although some of the steps in photosynthesis are still not completely understood, the overall photosynthetic equation has been known since the 19th century.
Label: Human

Text: Jan van Helmont began the research of the process in the mid-17th century when he carefully measured the mass of the soil a plant was using and the mass of the plant as it grew.
Label: Human

Text: After noticing that the soil mass changed very little, he hypothesized that the mass of the growing plant must come from the water, the only substance he added to the potted plant.
Label: Human

Text: His hypothesis was partially accurate – much of the gained mass comes from carbon dioxide as well as water.
Label: Human

Text: However, this was a signaling point to the idea that the bulk of a plant's biomass comes from the inputs of photosynthesis, not the soil itself.
Label: Human

Text: Joseph Priestley, a chemist and minister, discovered that when he isolated a volume of air under an inverted jar and burned a candle in it (which gave off CO2), the candle would burn out very quickly, much before it ran out of wax.
Label: Human

Text: He then showed that a plant could restore the air the candle and the mouse had "injured".
Label: Human

Text: He discovered that it was the influence of sunlight on the plant that could cause it to revive a mouse in a matter of hours.
Label: Human

Text: In 1796, Jean Senebier, a Swiss pastor, botanist, and naturalist, demonstrated that green plants consume carbon dioxide and release oxygen under the influence of light.
Label: Human

Text: Soon afterward, Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure showed that the increase in mass of the plant as it grows could not be due only to uptake of CO2 but also to the incorporation of water.
Label: Human

Text: Thus, the basic reaction by which organisms use photosynthesis to produce food (such as glucose) was outlined.
Label: Human

Text: Refinements Cornelis Van Niel made key discoveries explaining the chemistry of photosynthesis.
Label: Human

Text: By studying purple sulfur bacteria and green bacteria, he was the first to demonstrate that photosynthesis is a light-dependent redox reaction in which hydrogen reduces (donates its atoms as electrons and protons to) carbon dioxide.
Label: Human

Text: Robert Emerson discovered two light reactions by testing plant productivity using different wavelengths of light.
Label: Human

Text: Thus, there were two photosystems, one absorbing up to 600 nm wavelengths, the other up to 700 nm.
Label: Human

Text: PSI contains only chlorophyll "a", PSII contains primarily chlorophyll "a" with most of the available chlorophyll "b", among other pigments.
Label: Human

Text: These include phycobilins, which are the red and blue pigments of red and blue algae, respectively, and fucoxanthol for brown algae and diatoms.
Label: Human

Text: The process is most productive when the absorption of quanta is equal in both PSII and PSI, assuring that input energy from the antenna complex is divided between the PSI and PSII systems, which in turn powers the photochemistry.
Label: Human

Text: Robert Hill thought that a complex of reactions consisted of an intermediate to cytochrome b6 (now a plastoquinone), and that another was from cytochrome f to a step in the carbohydrate-generating mechanisms.
Label: Human

Text: These are linked by plastoquinone, which does require energy to reduce cytochrome f.
Label: Human

Text: Further experiments to prove that the oxygen developed during the photosynthesis of green plants came from water were performed by Hill in 1937 and 1939.
Label: Human

Text: He showed that isolated chloroplasts give off oxygen in the presence of unnatural reducing agents like iron oxalate, ferricyanide or benzoquinone after exposure to light.
Label: Human

Text: In the Hill reaction: 2 H2O + 2 A + (light, chloroplasts) → 2 AH2 + O2 A is the electron acceptor.
Label: Human

Text: Samuel Ruben and Martin Kamen used radioactive isotopes to determine that the oxygen liberated in photosynthesis came from the water.
Label: Human

Text: Melvin Calvin and Andrew Benson, along with James Bassham, elucidated the path of carbon assimilation (the photosynthetic carbon reduction cycle) in plants.
Label: Human

Text: The carbon reduction cycle is known as the Calvin cycle, but many scientists refer to it as the Calvin-Benson, Benson-Calvin, or even Calvin-Benson-Bassham (or CBB) Cycle.
Label: Human

Text: Marcus was later able to discover the function and significance of the electron transport chain.
Label: Human

Text: Otto Heinrich Warburg and Dean Burk discovered the I-quantum photosynthesis reaction that splits CO2, activated by the respiration.
Label: Human

Text: In 1950, first experimental evidence for the existence of photophosphorylation in vivo was presented by Otto Kandler using intact Chlorella cells and interpreting his findings as light-dependent ATP formation.
Label: Human

Text: Arnon et al. discovered photophosphorylation in vitro in isolated chloroplasts with the help of P32.
Label: Human

Text: Duysens and Jan Amesz discovered that chlorophyll "a" will absorb one light, oxidize cytochrome f, while chlorophyll "a" (and other pigments) will absorb another light but will reduce this same oxidized cytochrome, stating the two light reactions are in series.
Label: Human

Text: Development of the concept In 1893, the American botanist Charles Reid Barnes proposed two terms, photosyntax and photosynthesis, for the biological process of synthesis of complex carbon compounds out of carbonic acid, in the presence of chlorophyll, under the influence of light.
Label: Human

Text: The term photosynthesis is derived from the Greek phōs (φῶς, gleam) and sýnthesis (σύνθεσις, arranging together), while another word that he designated was photosyntax, from sýntaxis (σύνταξις, configuration).
Label: Human

Text: Later discovery of anoxygenic photosynthetic bacteria and photophosphorylation necessitated redefinition of the term.
Label: Human

Text: C3 : C4 photosynthesis research In the late 1940s at the University of California, Berkeley, the details of photosynthetic carbon metabolism were sorted out by the chemists Melvin Calvin, Andrew Benson, James Bassham and a score of students and researchers utilizing the carbon-14 isotope and paper chromatography techniques.
Label: Human

Text: The pathway of CO2 fixation by the algae Chlorella in a fraction of a second in light resulted in a three carbon molecule called phosphoglyceric acid (PGA).
Label: Human

Text: For that original and ground-breaking work, a Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Melvin Calvin in 1961.
Label: Human

Text: In parallel, plant physiologists studied leaf gas exchanges using the new method of infrared gas analysis and a leaf chamber where the net photosynthetic rates ranged from 10 to 13 μmol CO2·m−2·s−1, with the conclusion that all terrestrial plants have the same photosynthetic capacities, that are light saturated at less than 50% of sunlight.
Label: Human

Text: Later in 1958–1963 at Cornell University, field grown maize was reported to have much greater leaf photosynthetic rates of 40 μmol CO2·m−2·s−1 and not be saturated at near full sunlight.
Label: Human

Text: This higher rate in maize was almost double of those observed in other species such as wheat and soybean, indicating that large differences in photosynthesis exist among higher plants.
Label: Human

Text: At the University of Arizona, detailed gas exchange research on more than 15 species of monocots and dicots uncovered for the first time that differences in leaf anatomy are crucial factors in differentiating photosynthetic capacities among species.
Label: Human

Text: In tropical grasses, including maize, sorghum, sugarcane, Bermuda grass and in the dicot amaranthus, leaf photosynthetic rates were around 38−40 μmol CO2·m−2·s−1, and the leaves have two types of green cells, i.e. outer layer of mesophyll cells surrounding a tightly packed cholorophyllous vascular bundle sheath cells.
Label: Human

Text: This type of anatomy was termed Kranz anatomy in the 19th century by the botanist Gottlieb Haberlandt while studying leaf anatomy of sugarcane.
Label: Human

Text: Plant species with the greatest photosynthetic rates and Kranz anatomy showed no apparent photorespiration, very low CO2 compensation point, high optimum temperature, high stomatal resistances and lower mesophyll resistances for gas diffusion and rates never saturated at full sun light.
Label: Human

Text: These species were later termed C4 plants as the first stable compound of CO2 fixation in light has four carbons as malate and aspartate.
Label: Human

Text: Other species that lack Kranz anatomy were termed C3 type such as cotton and sunflower, as the first stable carbon compound is the three-carbon PGA.
Label: Human

Text: At 1000 ppm CO2 in measuring air, both the C3 and C4 plants had similar leaf photosynthetic rates around 60 μmol CO2·m−2·s−1 indicating the suppression of photorespiration in C3 plants.
Label: Human

Text: Factors There are four main factors influencing photosynthesis and several corollary factors.
Label: Human

Text: The four main are: Light irradiance and wavelength Water absorption Carbon dioxide concentration Temperature.
Label: Human

Text: These include the amount of light available, the amount of leaf area a plant has to capture light (shading by other plants is a major limitation of photosynthesis), the rate at which carbon dioxide can be supplied to the chloroplasts to support photosynthesis, the availability of water, and the availability of suitable temperatures for carrying out photosynthesis.
Label: Human

Text: Light intensity (irradiance), wavelength and temperature The process of photosynthesis provides the main input of free energy into the biosphere, and is one of four main ways in which radiation is important for plant life.
Label: Human

Text: The radiation climate within plant communities is extremely variable, in both time and space.
Label: Human

Text: In the early 20th century, Frederick Blackman and Gabrielle Matthaei investigated the effects of light intensity (irradiance) and temperature on the rate of carbon assimilation.
Label: Human

Text: At constant temperature, the rate of carbon assimilation varies with irradiance, increasing as the irradiance increases, but reaching a plateau at higher irradiance.
Label: Human

Text: At low irradiance, increasing the temperature has little influence on the rate of carbon assimilation.
Label: Human

Text: At constant high irradiance, the rate of carbon assimilation increases as the temperature is increased.
Label: Human

Text: These two experiments illustrate several important points: First, it is known that, in general, photochemical reactions are not affected by temperature.
Label: Human

Text: However, these experiments clearly show that temperature affects the rate of carbon assimilation, so there must be two sets of reactions in the full process of carbon assimilation.
Label: Human

Text: These are the light-dependent 'photochemical' temperature-independent stage, and the light-independent, temperature-dependent stage.
Label: Human

Text: Cyanobacteria, which reside several meters underwater, cannot receive the correct wavelengths required to cause photoinduced charge separation in conventional photosynthetic pigments.
Label: Human

Text: To combat this problem, Cyanobacteria have a light-harvesting complex called Phycobilisome.
Label: Human

Text: This complex is made up of a series of proteins with different pigments which surround the reaction center.
Label: Human

Text: Carbon dioxide levels and photorespiration As carbon dioxide concentrations rise, the rate at which sugars are made by the light-independent reactions increases until limited by other factors.
Label: Human

Text: RuBisCO, the enzyme that captures carbon dioxide in the light-independent reactions, has a binding affinity for both carbon dioxide and oxygen.
Label: Human

Text: When the concentration of carbon dioxide is high, RuBisCO will fix carbon dioxide.
Label: Human

Text: However, if the carbon dioxide concentration is low, RuBisCO will bind oxygen instead of carbon dioxide.
Label: Human

Text: This process, called photorespiration, uses energy, but does not produce sugars.
Label: Human

Text: RuBisCO oxygenase activity is disadvantageous to plants for several reasons: One product of oxygenase activity is phosphoglycolate (2 carbon) instead of 3-phosphoglycerate (3 carbon).
Label: Human

Text: Phosphoglycolate cannot be metabolized by the Calvin-Benson cycle and represents carbon lost from the cycle.
Label: Human

Text: A high oxygenase activity, therefore, drains the sugars that are required to recycle ribulose 5-bisphosphate and for the continuation of the Calvin-Benson cycle.
Label: Human

Text: Phosphoglycolate is quickly metabolized to glycolate that is toxic to a plant at a high concentration; it inhibits photosynthesis.
Label: Human

Text: Salvaging glycolate is an energetically expensive process that uses the glycolate pathway, and only 75% of the carbon is returned to the Calvin-Benson cycle as 3-phosphoglycerate.
Label: Human

Text: The reactions also produce ammonia (NH3), which is able to diffuse out of the plant, leading to a loss of nitrogen.
Label: Human

Text: A highly simplified summary is: 2 glycolate + ATP → 3-phosphoglycerate + carbon dioxide + ADP + NH3 The salvaging pathway for the products of RuBisCO oxygenase activity is more commonly known as photorespiration, since it is characterized by light-dependent oxygen consumption and the release of carbon dioxide.
Label: Human

Text: Evolution is the change in the heritable characteristics of biological populations over successive generations.
Label: Human

Text: It occurs when evolutionary processes such as genetic drift and natural selection act on genetic variation, resulting in certain characteristics becoming more or less common within a population over successive generations.
Label: Human

Text: The process of evolution has given rise to biodiversity at every level of biological organisation.
Label: Human

Text: The scientific theory of evolution by natural selection was conceived independently by two British naturalists, Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace, in the mid-19th century as an explanation for why organisms are adapted to their physical and biological environments.
Label: Human

Text: The theory was first set out in detail in Darwin's book On the Origin of Species.
Label: Human

Text: In successive generations, members of a population are therefore more likely to be replaced by the offspring of parents with favourable characteristics for that environment.
Label: Human

Text: In the early 20th century, competing ideas of evolution were refuted and evolution was combined with Mendelian inheritance and population genetics to give rise to modern evolutionary theory.
Label: Human

Text: In this synthesis the basis for heredity is in DNA molecules that pass information from generation to generation.
Label: Human

Text: The processes that change DNA in a population include natural selection, genetic drift, mutation, and gene flow.
Label: Human

Text: All life on Earth—including humanity—shares a last universal common ancestor (LUCA), which lived approximately 3.5–3.8 billion years ago.
Label: Human

Text: The fossil record includes a progression from early biogenic graphite to microbial mat fossils to fossilised multicellular organisms.
Label: Human

Text: Existing patterns of biodiversity have been shaped by repeated formations of new species (speciation), changes within species (anagenesis), and loss of species (extinction) throughout the evolutionary history of life on Earth.
Label: Human

Text: Morphological and biochemical traits tend to be more similar among species that share a more recent common ancestor, which historically was used to reconstruct phylogenetic trees, although direct comparison of genetic sequences is a more common method today.
Label: Human

Text: Evolutionary biologists have continued to study various aspects of evolution by forming and testing hypotheses as well as constructing theories based on evidence from the field or laboratory and on data generated by the methods of mathematical and theoretical biology.
Label: Human

Text: Their discoveries have influenced not just the development of biology but also other fields including agriculture, medicine, and computer science.
Label: Human

Text: Heredity Evolution in organisms occurs through changes in heritable characteristics—the inherited characteristics of an organism.
Label: Human

Text: In humans, for example, eye colour is an inherited characteristic and an individual might inherit the "brown-eye trait" from one of their parents.
Label: Human

Text: Inherited traits are controlled by genes and the complete set of genes within an organism's genome (genetic material) is called its genotype.
Label: Human

Text: The complete set of observable traits that make up the structure and behaviour of an organism is called its phenotype.
Label: Human

Text: Some of these traits come from the interaction of its genotype with the environment while others are neutral.
Label: Human

Text: For example, suntanned skin comes from the interaction between a person's genotype and sunlight; thus, suntans are not passed on to people's children.
Label: Human

Text: However, some people tan more easily than others, due to differences in genotypic variation; a striking example are people with the inherited trait of albinism, who do not tan at all and are very sensitive to sunburn.
Label: Human

Text: Heritable characteristics are passed from one generation to the next via DNA, a molecule that encodes genetic information.
Label: Human

Text: The sequence of bases along a particular DNA molecule specifies the genetic information, in a manner similar to a sequence of letters spelling out a sentence.
Label: Human

Text: Before a cell divides, the DNA is copied, so that each of the resulting two cells will inherit the DNA sequence.
Label: Human

Text: Portions of a DNA molecule that specify a single functional unit are called genes; different genes have different sequences of bases.
Label: Human

Text: The specific location of a DNA sequence within a chromosome is known as a locus.
Label: Human

Text: If the DNA sequence at a locus varies between individuals, the different forms of this sequence are called alleles.
Label: Human

Text: If a mutation occurs within a gene, the new allele may affect the trait that the gene controls, altering the phenotype of the organism.
Label: Human

Text: However, while this simple correspondence between an allele and a trait works in some cases, most traits are influenced by multiple genes in a quantitative or epistatic manner.
Label: Human

Text: Sources of variation Evolution can occur if there is genetic variation within a population.
Label: Human

Text: Variation comes from mutations in the genome, reshuffling of genes through sexual reproduction and migration between populations (gene flow).
Label: Human

Text: Despite the constant introduction of new variation through mutation and gene flow, most of the genome of a species is very similar among all individuals of that species.
Label: Human

Text: However, discoveries in the field of evolutionary developmental biology have demonstrated that even relatively small differences in genotype can lead to dramatic differences in phenotype both within and between species.
Label: Human

Text: An individual organism's phenotype results from both its genotype and the influence of the environment it has lived in.
Label: Human

Text: The modern evolutionary synthesis defines evolution as the change over time in this genetic variation.
Label: Human

Text: The frequency of one particular allele will become more or less prevalent relative to other forms of that gene.
Label: Human

Text: Variation disappears when a new allele reaches the point of fixation—when it either disappears from the population or replaces the ancestral allele entirely.
Label: Human

Text: Mutation Mutations are changes in the DNA sequence of a cell's genome and are the ultimate source of genetic variation in all organisms.
Label: Human

Text: When mutations occur, they may alter the product of a gene, or prevent the gene from functioning, or have no effect.
Label: Human

Text: About half of the mutations in the coding regions of protein-coding genes are deleterious — the other half are neutral.
Label: Human

Text: A small percentage of the total mutations in this region confer a fitness benefit.
Label: Human

Text: Some of the mutations in other parts of the genome are deleterious but the vast majority are neutral.
Label: Human

Text: Mutations can involve large sections of a chromosome becoming duplicated (usually by genetic recombination), which can introduce extra copies of a gene into a genome.
Label: Human

Text: Extra copies of genes are a major source of the raw material needed for new genes to evolve.
Label: Human

Text: This is important because most new genes evolve within gene families from pre-existing genes that share common ancestors.
Label: Human

Text: For example, the human eye uses four genes to make structures that sense light: three for colour vision and one for night vision; all four are descended from a single ancestral gene.
Label: Human

Text: New genes can be generated from an ancestral gene when a duplicate copy mutates and acquires a new function.
Label: Human

Text: This process is easier once a gene has been duplicated because it increases the redundancy of the system; one gene in the pair can acquire a new function while the other copy continues to perform its original function.
Label: Human

Text: Other types of mutations can even generate entirely new genes from previously noncoding DNA, a phenomenon termed de novo gene birth.
Label: Human

Text: The generation of new genes can also involve small parts of several genes being duplicated, with these fragments then recombining to form new combinations with new functions (exon shuffling).
Label: Human

Text: When new genes are assembled from shuffling pre-existing parts, domains act as modules with simple independent functions, which can be mixed together to produce new combinations with new and complex functions.
Label: Human

Text: For example, polyketide synthases are large enzymes that make antibiotics; they contain up to 100 independent domains that each catalyse one step in the overall process, like a step in an assembly line.
Label: Human

Text: They are camouflage coloured and show a characteristic pattern of dark and light longitudinal stripes.
Label: Human

Text: The majority of pig breeds carry MC1R mutations disrupting wild-type colour and different mutations causing dominant black colouring.
Label: Human

Text: Sex and recombination In asexual organisms, genes are inherited together, or linked, as they cannot mix with genes of other organisms during reproduction.
Label: Human

Text: In contrast, the offspring of sexual organisms contain random mixtures of their parents' chromosomes that are produced through independent assortment.
Label: Human

Text: In a related process called homologous recombination, sexual organisms exchange DNA between two matching chromosomes.
Label: Human

Text: Recombination and reassortment do not alter allele frequencies, but instead change which alleles are associated with each other, producing offspring with new combinations of alleles.
Label: Human

Text: The first cost is that in sexually dimorphic species only one of the two sexes can bear young.
Label: Human

Text: This cost does not apply to hermaphroditic species, like most plants and many invertebrates.
Label: Human

Text: The second cost is that any individual who reproduces sexually can only pass on 50% of its genes to any individual offspring, with even less passed on as each new generation passes.
Label: Human

Text: Yet sexual reproduction is the more common means of reproduction among eukaryotes and multicellular organisms.
Label: Human

Text: The Red Queen hypothesis has been used to explain the significance of sexual reproduction as a means to enable continual evolution and adaptation in response to coevolution with other species in an ever-changing environment.
Label: Human

Text: Another hypothesis is that sexual reproduction is primarily an adaptation for promoting accurate recombinational repair of damage in germline DNA, and that increased diversity is a byproduct of this process that may sometimes be adaptively beneficial.
Label: Human

Text: Gene flow Gene flow is the exchange of genes between populations and between species.
Label: Human

Text: It can therefore be a source of variation that is new to a population or to a species.
Label: Human

Text: Gene flow can be caused by the movement of individuals between separate populations of organisms, as might be caused by the movement of mice between inland and coastal populations, or the movement of pollen between heavy-metal-tolerant and heavy-metal-sensitive populations of grasses.
Label: Human

Text: Gene transfer between species includes the formation of hybrid organisms and horizontal gene transfer.
Label: Human

Text: Horizontal gene transfer is the transfer of genetic material from one organism to another organism that is not its offspring; this is most common among bacteria.
Label: Human

Text: In medicine, this contributes to the spread of antibiotic resistance, as when one bacteria acquires resistance genes it can rapidly transfer them to other species.
Label: Human

Text: Horizontal transfer of genes from bacteria to eukaryotes such as the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae and the adzuki bean weevil Callosobruchus chinensis has occurred.
Label: Human

Text: An example of larger-scale transfers are the eukaryotic bdelloid rotifers, which have received a range of genes from bacteria, fungi and plants.
Label: Human

Text: Viruses can also carry DNA between organisms, allowing transfer of genes even across biological domains.
Label: Human

Text: Large-scale gene transfer has also occurred between the ancestors of eukaryotic cells and bacteria, during the acquisition of chloroplasts and mitochondria.
Label: Human

Text: It is possible that eukaryotes themselves originated from horizontal gene transfers between bacteria and archaea.
Label: Human

Text: Epigenetics Some heritable changes cannot be explained by changes to the sequence of nucleotides in the DNA.
Label: Human

Text: DNA methylation marking chromatin, self-sustaining metabolic loops, gene silencing by RNA interference and the three-dimensional conformation of proteins (such as prions) are areas where epigenetic inheritance systems have been discovered at the organismic level.
Label: Human

Text: Developmental biologists suggest that complex interactions in genetic networks and communication among cells can lead to heritable variations that may underlay some of the mechanics in developmental plasticity and canalisation.
Label: Human

Text: For example, ecological inheritance through the process of niche construction is defined by the regular and repeated activities of organisms in their environment.
Label: Human

Text: This generates a legacy of effects that modify and feed back into the selection regime of subsequent generations.
Label: Human

Text: Other examples of heritability in evolution that are not under the direct control of genes include the inheritance of cultural traits and symbiogenesis.
Label: Human

Text: Evolutionary forces From a neo-Darwinian perspective, evolution occurs when there are changes in the frequencies of alleles within a population of interbreeding organisms, for example, the allele for black colour in a population of moths becoming more common.
Label: Human

Text: Mechanisms that can lead to changes in allele frequencies include natural selection, genetic drift, and mutation bias.
Label: Human

Text: Natural selection Evolution by natural selection is the process by which traits that enhance survival and reproduction become more common in successive generations of a population.
Label: Human

Text: It embodies three principles: Variation exists within populations of organisms with respect to morphology, physiology and behaviour (phenotypic variation).
Label: Human

Text: Different traits confer different rates of survival and reproduction (differential fitness).
Label: Human

Text: These traits can be passed from generation to generation (heritability of fitness).
Label: Human

Text: More offspring are produced than can possibly survive, and these conditions produce competition between organisms for survival and reproduction.
Label: Human

Text: Consequently, organisms with traits that give them an advantage over their competitors are more likely to pass on their traits to the next generation than those with traits that do not confer an advantage.
Label: Human

Text: This teleonomy is the quality whereby the process of natural selection creates and preserves traits that are seemingly fitted for the functional roles they perform.
Label: Human

Text: The central concept of natural selection is the evolutionary fitness of an organism.
Label: Human

Text: Fitness is measured by an organism's ability to survive and reproduce, which determines the size of its genetic contribution to the next generation.
Label: Human

Text: However, fitness is not the same as the total number of offspring: instead fitness is indicated by the proportion of subsequent generations that carry an organism's genes.
Label: Human

Text: For example, if an organism could survive well and reproduce rapidly, but its offspring were all too small and weak to survive, this organism would make little genetic contribution to future generations and would thus have low fitness.
Label: Human

Text: If an allele increases fitness more than the other alleles of that gene, then with each generation this allele has a higher probability of becoming common within the population.
Label: Human

Text: Examples of traits that can increase fitness are enhanced survival and increased fecundity.
Label: Human

Text: Conversely, the lower fitness caused by having a less beneficial or deleterious allele results in this allele likely becoming rarer—they are selected against.
Label: Human

Text: Importantly, the fitness of an allele is not a fixed characteristic; if the environment changes, previously neutral or harmful traits may become beneficial and previously beneficial traits become harmful.
Label: Human

Text: However, even if the direction of selection does reverse in this way, traits that were lost in the past may not re-evolve in an identical form.
Label: Human

Text: However, a re-activation of dormant genes, as long as they have not been eliminated from the genome and were only suppressed perhaps for hundreds of generations, can lead to the re-occurrence of traits thought to be lost like hindlegs in dolphins, teeth in chickens, wings in wingless stick insects, tails and additional nipples in humans etc. "Throwbacks" such as these are known as atavisms.
Label: Human

Text: Natural selection within a population for a trait that can vary across a range of values, such as height, can be categorised into three different types.
Label: Human

Text: The first is directional selection, which is a shift in the average value of a trait over time—for example, organisms slowly getting taller.
Label: Human

Text: Secondly, disruptive selection is selection for extreme trait values and often results in two different values becoming most common, with selection against the average value.
Label: Human

Text: This would be when either short or tall organisms had an advantage, but not those of medium height.
Label: Human

Text: Finally, in stabilising selection there is selection against extreme trait values on both ends, which causes a decrease in variance around the average value and less diversity.
Label: Human

Text: Natural selection most generally makes nature the measure against which individuals and individual traits, are more or less likely to survive. "Nature" in this sense refers to an ecosystem, that is, a system in which organisms interact with every other element, physical as well as biological, in their local environment.
Label: Human

Text: These relationships involve the life history of the organism, its position in the food chain and its geographic range.
Label: Human

Text: This broad understanding of nature enables scientists to delineate specific forces which, together, comprise natural selection.
Label: Human

Text: Natural selection can act at different levels of organisation, such as genes, cells, individual organisms, groups of organisms and species.
Label: Human

Text: An example of selection occurring below the level of the individual organism are genes called transposons, which can replicate and spread throughout a genome.
Label: Human

Text: Selection at a level above the individual, such as group selection, may allow the evolution of cooperation.
Label: Human

Text: Genetic drift Genetic drift is the random fluctuation of allele frequencies within a population from one generation to the next.
Label: Human

Text: When selective forces are absent or relatively weak, allele frequencies are equally likely to drift upward or downward in each successive generation because the alleles are subject to sampling error.
Label: Human

Text: This drift halts when an allele eventually becomes fixed, either by disappearing from the population or by replacing the other alleles entirely.
Label: Human

Text: Genetic drift may therefore eliminate some alleles from a population due to chance alone.
Label: Human

Text: Even in the absence of selective forces, genetic drift can cause two separate populations that begin with the same genetic structure to drift apart into two divergent populations with different sets of alleles.
Label: Human

Text: According to the neutral theory of molecular evolution most evolutionary changes are the result of the fixation of neutral mutations by genetic drift.
Label: Human

Text: In this model, most genetic changes in a population are thus the result of constant mutation pressure and genetic drift.
Label: Human

Text: This form of the neutral theory has been debated since it does not seem to fit some genetic variation seen in nature.
Label: Human

Text: A better-supported version of this model is the nearly neutral theory, according to which a mutation that would be effectively neutral in a small population is not necessarily neutral in a large population.
Label: Human

Text: Other theories propose that genetic drift is dwarfed by other stochastic forces in evolution, such as genetic hitchhiking, also known as genetic draft.
Label: Human

Text: Another concept is constructive neutral evolution (CNE), which explains that complex systems can emerge and spread into a population through neutral transitions due to the principles of excess capacity, presuppression, and ratcheting, and it has been applied in areas ranging from the origins of the spliceosome to the complex interdependence of microbial communities.
Label: Human

Text: The time it takes a neutral allele to become fixed by genetic drift depends on population size; fixation is more rapid in smaller populations.
Label: Human

Text: The number of individuals in a population is not critical, but instead a measure known as the effective population size.
Label: Human

Text: The effective population is usually smaller than the total population since it takes into account factors such as the level of inbreeding and the stage of the lifecycle in which the population is the smallest.
Label: Human

Text: The effective population size may not be the same for every gene in the same population.
Label: Human

Text: It is usually difficult to measure the relative importance of selection and neutral processes, including drift.
Label: Human

Text: The comparative importance of adaptive and non-adaptive forces in driving evolutionary change is an area of current research.
Label: Human

Text: Mutation bias Mutation bias is usually conceived as a difference in expected rates for two different kinds of mutation, e.g., transition-transversion bias, GC-AT bias, deletion-insertion bias.
Label: Human

Text: Haldane and Ronald Fisher argued that, because mutation is a weak pressure easily overcome by selection, tendencies of mutation would be ineffectual except under conditions of neutral evolution or extraordinarily high mutation rates.
Label: Human

Text: This opposing-pressures argument was long used to dismiss the possibility of internal tendencies in evolution, until the molecular era prompted renewed interest in neutral evolution.
Label: Human

Text: Noboru Sueoka and Ernst Freese proposed that systematic biases in mutation might be responsible for systematic differences in genomic GC composition between species.
Label: Human

Text: The identification of a GC-biased E. coli mutator strain in 1967, along with the proposal of the neutral theory, established the plausibility of mutational explanations for molecular patterns, which are now common in the molecular evolution literature.
Label: Human

Text: Such models also include effects of selection, following the mutation-selection-drift model, which allows both for mutation biases and differential selection based on effects on translation.
Label: Human

Text: Hypotheses of mutation bias have played an important role in the development of thinking about the evolution of genome composition, including isochores.
Label: Human

Text: Different insertion vs. deletion biases in different taxa can lead to the evolution of different genome sizes.
Label: Human

Text: The hypothesis of Lynch regarding genome size relies on mutational biases toward increase or decrease in genome size.
Label: Human

Text: However, mutational hypotheses for the evolution of composition suffered a reduction in scope when it was discovered that (1) GC-biased gene conversion makes an important contribution to composition in diploid organisms such as mammals and (2) bacterial genomes frequently have AT-biased mutation.
Label: Human

Text: Contemporary thinking about the role of mutation biases reflects a different theory from that of Haldane and Fisher.
Label: Human

Text: More recent work showed that the original "pressures" theory assumes that evolution is based on standing variation: when evolution depends on events of mutation that introduce new alleles, mutational and developmental biases in the introduction of variation (arrival biases) can impose biases on evolution without requiring neutral evolution or high mutation rates.
Label: Human

Text: Several studies report that the mutations implicated in adaptation reflect common mutation biases though others dispute this interpretation.
Label: Human

Text: Genetic hitchhiking Recombination allows alleles on the same strand of DNA to become separated.
Label: Human

Text: However, the rate of recombination is low (approximately two events per chromosome per generation).
Label: Human

Text: As a result, genes close together on a chromosome may not always be shuffled away from each other and genes that are close together tend to be inherited together, a phenomenon known as linkage.
Label: Human

Text: This tendency is measured by finding how often two alleles occur together on a single chromosome compared to expectations, which is called their linkage disequilibrium.
Label: Human

Text: This can be important when one allele in a particular haplotype is strongly beneficial: natural selection can drive a selective sweep that will also cause the other alleles in the haplotype to become more common in the population; this effect is called genetic hitchhiking or genetic draft.
Label: Human

Text: Genetic draft caused by the fact that some neutral genes are genetically linked to others that are under selection can be partially captured by an appropriate effective population size.
Label: Human

Text: Sexual selection A special case of natural selection is sexual selection, which is selection for any trait that increases mating success by increasing the attractiveness of an organism to potential mates.
Label: Human

Text: Traits that evolved through sexual selection are particularly prominent among males of several animal species.
Label: Human

Text: Although sexually favoured, traits such as cumbersome antlers, mating calls, large body size and bright colours often attract predation, which compromises the survival of individual males.
Label: Human

Text: This survival disadvantage is balanced by higher reproductive success in males that show these hard-to-fake, sexually selected traits.
Label: Human

Text: Natural outcomes Evolution influences every aspect of the form and behaviour of organisms.
Label: Human

Text: Most prominent are the specific behavioural and physical adaptations that are the outcome of natural selection.
Label: Human

Text: These adaptations increase fitness by aiding activities such as finding food, avoiding predators or attracting mates.
